0.title: Amos: Let Justice Roll Down
0.overview:
The message. Amos is God’s word to a comfortable, religious nation. Israel was rich and busy at worship, sure that God was on its side; but the people who crowded the shrines were crushing the poor, and God will not take worship from hands that oppress: “let justice roll down like waters, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream” (5:24). Privilege does not shield a people from judgment; it makes them more accountable: “You only have I known of all the families of the earth; therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities” (3:2). Yet through the roar of judgment God still calls, “Seek me and live” (5:4), and the book ends with the fallen house of David raised up and God’s people planted where “they shall never again be uprooted” (9:15).

Background: the prophet. Amos was no preacher by trade but a man “among the shepherds of Tekoa” (1:1), a small town in the hills of Judah. When the priest of Bethel tried to send him home, he answered, “I was no prophet, nor a prophet’s son, but I was a herdsman and a dresser of sycamore figs. But the LORD took me from following the flock” (7:14–15). A man of Judah, paid by no shrine, he was sent north to the kingdom of Israel. Many modern scholars think later editors added the hopeful ending (9:11–15), since “the booth of David that is fallen” seems to look back on Jerusalem’s fall in 586 BC. But the prophets regularly saw past judgment to mercy (Hosea 3:5), and David’s house had already lost ten tribes. This commentary takes the whole book as Amos’s own.

When and where. Amos preached about 760 BC, “in the days of Uzziah king of Judah and in the days of Jeroboam the son of Joash, king of Israel, two years before the earthquake” (1:1). Since the kingdom split, the north had worshipped at the golden calves Jeroboam son of Nebat set up at Bethel and Dan (1 Kings 12:28–29). Now, under Jeroboam II, Israel was at its height. With Assyria held back for a time by troubles of its own, he “restored the border of Israel from Lebo-hamath as far as the Sea of the Arabah”, as Jonah had foretold (2 Kings 14:25). Hosea preached in the north soon after, and Isaiah and Micah in Judah. Within about forty years Assyria returned in strength, and in 722 BC Samaria fell and its people were carried away (2 Kings 17:5–6).

The world of the book. It was a golden age for those at the top, with “the winter house along with the summer house” and “houses of ivory” (3:15); excavators at Samaria have found hundreds of carved ivory pieces from furniture. But the wealth was built on the poor. The powerful would “sell the righteous for silver, and the needy for a pair of sandals” (2:6). Judges in the city gate took bribes (5:12), and merchants longed for the new moon and the Sabbath to be over, “that we may make the ephah small and the shekel great and deal deceitfully with false balances” (8:5). Meanwhile the shrines were full. Israel took its prosperity as proof of God’s favour, and longed for “the day of the LORD” to crown its success (5:18).

The kind of writing. Amos is prophecy, almost all in Hebrew poetry, with pictures from the farm and the wild: a roaring lion, a bird in a snare, a basket of summer fruit, whose Hebrew name sounds like “the end” (8:1–2). He sings a funeral song over a nation still alive (5:1–2), and three times breaks into a hymn to the Creator (4:13; 5:8–9; 9:5–6).

How the book makes its case. The theme comes first: “The LORD roars from Zion” (1:2). Then Amos condemns Israel’s neighbours one by one for cruelty even pagans knew was wrong, then Judah, and, as his hearers cheer, closes the circle on Israel itself with the longest charge of all (1–2). His sermons press it home (3–6): God sent famine, drought and plague, “yet you did not return to me” (4:6–11); the day of the LORD will be “darkness, and not light” (5:18); those “at ease in Zion” will be the first into exile (6:1, 7). Then come five visions (7–9): locusts and fire, held back when Amos prays; a plumb line showing the wall is crooked; ripe fruit; and the Lord at the altar, bringing it down. Between them the priest Amaziah orders Amos out of “the king’s sanctuary” (7:10–17), proving that Israel would not hear. Only at the end does the darkness break: God will sift his people but not destroy them utterly, raise up David’s fallen booth, gather the nations, and plant his people in a land of endless harvest (9:8–15).

Is Amos a manifesto for social justice? Some make Amos a political reformer; others read past him as if God cared only about private faith. Amos allows neither. Cruelty and cheating are sins against God himself. But the root of Israel’s injustice was that it had forgotten the God who brought it out of Egypt (2:10), and the cure he offers is first not a policy but himself (5:4–6). This commentary’s view is that the church must preach God’s whole law, which has public weight, and Christians must care for the poor and deal honestly; but Amos hands us no party programme, and faithful Christians may differ about policy while agreeing that God hates oppression.

Where it leads: to Christ. Amos leads to Christ by the need he exposes and by promise. His plumb line shows that none of us is straight; Christ alone loved God and neighbour perfectly, and his righteousness covers all who trust him. Amos pleaded for a people who rejected him (7:1–6); Christ “always lives to make intercession” for his own (Hebrews 7:25). Amos warned that God would “make the sun go down at noon” with mourning “like the mourning for an only son” (8:9–10); those words found a deeper echo when “there was darkness over the whole land” (Luke 23:44) and God’s only Son bore the judgment his people deserved. And the promise of David’s booth was kept when God raised Jesus, David’s Son, to reign. James quoted it, from the Greek version, to show that Gentiles believing in Jesus was God’s plan: “I will rebuild the tent of David that has fallen … that the remnant of mankind may seek the Lord, and all the Gentiles who are called by my name” (Acts 15:16–17). The Lord who roars from Zion has come as “the Lion of the tribe of Judah” (Revelation 5:5), and he is the Lamb who was slain.

Where Christians differ. Many dispensational Christians expect the closing promises of land and harvest to be fulfilled in a future earthly kingdom for Israel. This commentary’s view, with many in the Reformed tradition, is that they are fulfilled in Christ’s present reign as he gathers the nations and completed in the new creation; the modern state of Israel is not their fulfilment, though Christians should love the Jewish people and pray for their salvation. All agree that God’s last word is not judgment but grace.

For us. Amos still roars at comfortable, religious people. Is our worship on Sunday matched by how we treat the poor, our workers and our customers on Monday? Are we “at ease in Zion”, untouched by the ruin of others? None of us passes his plumb line, and the gospel does not lower it; it sends us to Christ, who met it for us and bore our judgment. Forgiven people then begin to love what God loves: honest dealing, open hands and justice for the weak. And to every generation Amos holds out God’s invitation: “Seek the LORD and live” (5:6).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–2 — The LORD Roars from Zion
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before a single nation is named, the book tells us who is speaking and with what force. These are the words of Amos, a herdsman from Tekoa in Judah, given to him by God and set in a dated moment of history: the prosperous reigns of Uzziah and Jeroboam, two years before an earthquake no one forgot (v. 1). Then the theme of the whole book comes in one line of poetry. The LORD roars from Zion like a lion over its prey, and the land withers under his voice, from the shepherds’ pastures in the south to the green top of Carmel in the north (v. 2). Israel’s God is not a tame deity kept at its shrines; when he speaks, the whole land feels it.
verseByVerse.theology: God is not silent. When he speaks in judgment, the whole land feels it.

verseByVerse.quote: The words of Amos, who was among the shepherds of Tekoa, which he saw concerning Israel in the days of Uzziah king of Judah and in the days of Jeroboam the son of Joash, king of Israel, two years before the earthquake.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These are God’s words, given to an ordinary working man from Judah at a real moment in history. Amos did not invent his message; he “saw” it, shown to him by God, and the book dates it by an earthquake everyone remembered.

Among the shepherds of Tekoa. Amos was not a professional prophet. Tekoa was a small town in the hills of Judah, about ten miles south of Jerusalem, and he was also “a dresser of sycamore figs” (7:14): a working man from the southern kingdom, sent north to Israel. His words, full of a shepherd’s vocabulary, are still God’s word (2 Peter 1:21).

In the days of Uzziah … and … Jeroboam. About 760 BC, under Jeroboam II, Israel was at its height (see the introduction and Kings of Israel and Judah), and people felt God was plainly on their side.

Two years before the earthquake. The earthquake was still spoken of centuries later: “you shall flee as you fled from the earthquake in the days of Uzziah king of Judah” (Zechariah 14:5). When the ground shook, it must have seemed to confirm his warnings.

A word rooted in history. The God who spoke through a herdsman at a dated moment has spoken at last “by his Son” (Hebrews 1:2), also under named rulers (Luke 3:1–2): not myth, but news.

Uncertain wording. The word for “shepherds” is rare; elsewhere it describes only Mesha king of Moab, “a sheep breeder” (2 Kings 3:4), so Amos may have owned or managed flocks rather than simply tending them (as the ESV notes). And “two years before the earthquake” could mean “during two years” (also an ESV note).
verseByVerse.note: Tekoa, on the edge of the Judean wilderness, was also the home of the wise woman Joab sent for in 2 Samuel 14:2.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said: "The LORD roars from Zion and utters his voice from Jerusalem; the pastures of the shepherds mourn, and the top of Carmel withers."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel’s God speaks in judgment, and his voice is as terrifying and unmistakable as a lion’s roar. This verse is the theme of the whole book.

The LORD roars from Zion. A shepherd knows what a roar means: the lion is close, and it has found its prey (3:4, 8). Now it is the LORD who roars. Joel uses the same words (Joel 3:16), but there the roar falls on the nations while the LORD shelters his people; here it is turned against Israel.

Utters his voice from Jerusalem. The northern kingdom had broken away from Jerusalem and set up its own shrines at Bethel and Dan (1 Kings 12:28–29). Amos reminds them that the true God still speaks from the place he chose, the city of David’s royal line and of the temple. Their shrines cannot silence him.

The top of Carmel withers. From the southern pastures where Amos worked to Carmel, the green ridge on the northern coast, everything dries up, and the pastures “mourn”. When God speaks in judgment, creation itself goes into mourning.

The Lion who is the Lamb. God is no tame voice to be safely ignored. This Lord has come to us in Jesus Christ, “the Lion of the tribe of Judah” (Revelation 5:5). Yet when John turned to see the Lion, he saw “a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain” (Revelation 5:6). The Lord who roars in judgment is the Shepherd who laid down his life for his sheep, and we must hear both.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God holds nations that never had his written law accountable for cruelty every conscience condemns. Each oracle follows one pattern: sin piled beyond the full measure (“for three … and for four”), one representative crime, and fire on the guilty nation’s strongholds. Damascus dragged iron threshing sledges over the people of Gilead, so its dynasty will burn and its people be sent back to Kir (vv. 3–5). Gaza raided whole communities and sold them on to Edom, and every Philistine city will fall with it (vv. 6–8). Tyre did the same, and broke a covenant of brotherhood besides (vv. 9–10). Violence against people, trade in people and broken faith with people are all sins against the God whose image they bear.
verseByVerse.theology: God holds even nations without his written law accountable for cruelty to other human beings.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "For three transgressions of Damascus, and for four, I will not revoke the punishment, because they have threshed Gilead with threshing sledges of iron. So I will send a fire upon the house of Hazael, and it shall devour the strongholds of Ben-hadad. I will break the gate-bar of Damascus, and cut off the inhabitants from the Valley of Aven, and him who holds the scepter from Beth-eden; and the people of Syria shall go into exile to Kir," says the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Damascus has piled up sin beyond the full measure by crushing the people of Gilead like grain, and God’s judgment on it can no longer be turned back.

For three transgressions of Damascus, and for four. Each of the eight oracles opens this way, a common form of Hebrew poetry (compare “Three things are too wonderful for me; four I do not understand”, Proverbs 30:18). It does not count sins exactly. Three would already be enough; the fourth is one more on top. Sin has run past the full measure, and God’s patience has run its course. Usually only one sin is then named, the one that shows the nation’s heart.

I will not revoke the punishment. Literally “I will not turn it back” (as the ESV notes): the judgment has already left the bow.

They have threshed Gilead. Damascus was the capital of Syria (also called Aram), Israel’s northern neighbour and bitter enemy; Gilead was Israelite land east of the Jordan. Threshing sledges were heavy boards studded underneath with iron or stone, dragged over grain to break it (see threshing floor). Damascus treated human beings like grain: the king of Syria had made Israel’s army “like the dust at threshing” (2 Kings 13:7).

The house of Hazael. Hazael seized Syria’s throne and waged brutal war on Israel. When Elisha foresaw it, he wept: “I know the evil that you will do to the people of Israel” (2 Kings 8:12). Ben-hadad was his son and successor. The fire is the burning of cities in war, and God sends it, even when human armies carry it.

The people of Syria shall go into exile to Kir. The bar that locked the city gate will be smashed, and “him who holds the scepter”, the ruler, cut off. Later Amos says that God brought the Syrians “from Kir” (9:7); now he will send them back, as if their history as a nation were being undone. Within a few decades it happened: “The king of Assyria marched up against Damascus and took it, carrying its people captive to Kir” (2 Kings 16:9).

Patience with a limit. “For three … and for four” means that God had waited, as he still waits, “not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance” (2 Peter 3:9). His patience holds the door open to Christ, but not for ever.

Uncertain wording. The Valley of Aven (“valley of wickedness”, perhaps a mocking name; the ESV notes the reading “On”) and Beth-eden (“house of delight”) were places in the Syrian kingdom, but where exactly is uncertain (some suggest the Beqaa valley in Lebanon, and an Aramean state on the Euphrates). The point is plain: from the valley floor to the ruler’s seat, Syria will be emptied.
verseByVerse.note: The refrain sounds eight times, once for each nation in chapters 1 and 2, ending with Israel.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "For three transgressions of Gaza, and for four, I will not revoke the punishment, because they carried into exile a whole people to deliver them up to Edom. So I will send a fire upon the wall of Gaza, and it shall devour her strongholds. I will cut off the inhabitants from Ashdod, and him who holds the scepter from Ashkelon; I will turn my hand against Ekron, and the remnant of the Philistines shall perish," says the Lord GOD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gaza raided whole communities and sold them as slaves, so God will sweep away every Philistine city as they swept away others.

They carried into exile a whole people. Gaza, a chief Philistine city south-west of Judah, committed slave trading on a massive scale, probably raiding whole villages and selling everyone to Edom, to be passed on along the trade routes. Joel brings a similar charge against the Philistines (Joel 3:4–6).

I will cut off the inhabitants from Ashdod. The judgment spreads from Gaza to Ashdod, Ashkelon and Ekron. Gath, the fifth of the famous Philistine cities, is not named; it may already have been weakened, since Uzziah “broke through the wall of Gath” (2 Chronicles 26:6). Down to “the remnant”, the last survivors, the people who swept away whole communities will be swept away.

Why the nations are accountable. God never gave the Philistines the Ten Commandments, yet he holds them responsible. Every person bears his image (Genesis 9:6), and every conscience knows that selling people like cattle is wicked. Even those without the written law show “that the work of the law is written on their hearts” (Romans 2:15).

Who are we to judge another culture? It is a respectable instinct of our time. But try saying it to the villages Gaza emptied: our relativism runs out the moment someone is sold. Amos assumes what every conscience assumes: there is a moral law above every culture, and every nation will answer to it. That is not arrogance, for Amos is about to turn the same searchlight on his own people (2:4–8), and it is the only ground on which the weak can appeal against the strong. The trade has not ended, and the God who saw Gaza sees the millions held in forced labour and sexual exploitation today. Yet a law above all cultures condemns all cultures, ours included. The good news is that the Judge of the nations is the Lamb who was slain to ransom people “from every tribe and language and people and nation” (Revelation 5:9).

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "For three transgressions of Tyre, and for four, I will not revoke the punishment, because they delivered up a whole people to Edom, and did not remember the covenant of brotherhood. So I will send a fire upon the wall of Tyre, and it shall devour her strongholds."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tyre joined the slave trade and betrayed a sworn friendship, and no wall can keep out the fire God sends.

Did not remember the covenant of brotherhood. Tyre, the great trading port of Phoenicia north of Israel, trafficked in people like Gaza, and added a further sin: it betrayed people it was bound to by a solemn agreement (see the box below). A broken oath is a sin God sees, even between nations.

A fire upon the wall of Tyre. Much of Tyre stood on an island and held out against great empires for years. But no wall keeps out the fire God sends. Ezekiel too foretold its fall (Ezekiel 26), and Alexander the Great finally took it in 332 BC by building a causeway to the island.

The Brother who keeps covenant. Tyre forgot its brother; Christ “is not ashamed to call them brothers” (Hebrews 2:11) and kept his covenant at the cost of his blood. Yet Jesus said it would be “more bearable on the day of judgment for Tyre and Sidon” than for towns that saw his works and did not repent (Matthew 11:22): those who know more answer for more, as Amos is about to tell Israel.

Uncertain wording. Which covenant is meant is not certain. Most think of the old friendship between Tyre and Israel: Hiram of Tyre and Solomon “made a treaty” (1 Kings 5:12), and Hiram called Solomon “my brother” (1 Kings 9:13). Others think of a treaty with Edom or other neighbours. Either way, Tyre broke its word to sell human beings.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: No hatred is hidden from God, and no ambition excuses cruelty to the helpless. Edom, descended from Esau, hunted his brother Israel with the sword, deliberately smothering every feeling of pity, and kept his anger alive from one generation to the next; fire will fall on Teman and Bozrah (vv. 11–12). Ammon committed the most horrifying crime in the chapter: in its wars over Gilead it ripped open pregnant women, killing mothers and unborn children together to push a border a few miles further. Its capital will burn amid the shouts of battle and the storm of God’s judgment, and its king and princes will go into exile together (vv. 13–15). By now Amos’s hearers are cheering, unaware that the circle is closing round them.
verseByVerse.theology: No hatred is hidden from God, and no ambition justifies cruelty to the helpless.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "For three transgressions of Edom, and for four, I will not revoke the punishment, because he pursued his brother with the sword and cast off all pity, and his anger tore perpetually, and he kept his wrath forever. So I will send a fire upon Teman, and it shall devour the strongholds of Bozrah."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Edom kept a family hatred burning for generations and hunted his brother with the sword, so God’s fire will answer the fire of his anger.

He pursued his brother with the sword. Edom lay south-east of Judah, and its people descended from Esau, twin brother of Jacob (Israel); that is why God speaks of “his brother”. Moses once greeted the king of Edom with the words “Thus says your brother Israel” (Numbers 20:14), but the relationship became a long feud.

Cast off all pity. Edom deliberately shut down every feeling of compassion. “His anger tore perpetually”, like a wild animal that keeps tearing at its prey, and “he kept his wrath forever”, nursing a grudge from generation to generation. This is a portrait of bitterness: it begins in the heart and ends with the sword. Obadiah condemned Edom for the same thing: “Because of the violence done to your brother Jacob, shame shall cover you” (Obadiah 10).

A fire upon Teman. Teman and Bozrah stand for the whole nation. The fire of Edom’s anger will be answered by the fire of God’s judgment.

The Brother who kept no wrath. Edom kept his wrath for ever; the Son of God came to brothers who had wronged him, bore the wrath that was ours, and prayed, “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34). The gospel is the only power that can end an old feud.

Bitterness today. Families, churches and friends can keep a grudge alive for years. Jesus teaches us to forgive “from your heart”, as we have been forgiven (Matthew 18:35). That does not mean pretending no wrong was done or returning to someone still dangerous; it means handing the debt to God (Romans 12:19) and refusing to keep the anger alive.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "For three transgressions of the Ammonites, and for four, I will not revoke the punishment, because they have ripped open pregnant women in Gilead, that they might enlarge their border. So I will kindle a fire in the wall of Rabbah, and it shall devour her strongholds, with shouting on the day of battle, with a tempest in the day of the whirlwind; and their king shall go into exile, he and his princes together," says the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ammon slaughtered mothers and unborn children to push its border further, and God, who sees the unborn, will send its king into exile.

They have ripped open pregnant women in Gilead. The Ammonites lived east of the Jordan, next to Israel’s territory in Gilead. In war they ripped open pregnant women, killing mothers and unborn children together. The reason is chillingly simple: “that they might enlarge their border”. For more land they would wipe out Gilead’s next generation. Elisha foresaw the same atrocity from Hazael (2 Kings 8:12), and within a few years Israel’s own king Menahem would commit it (2 Kings 15:16).

A fire in the wall of Rabbah. Rabbah was Ammon’s capital, the site of modern Amman in Jordan. Judgment comes with the shouts of soldiers storming the city, but behind them, like “a tempest” and “the whirlwind”, stands the irresistible power of God.

Their king shall go into exile. The planners of the atrocities go too, “he and his princes together” (the ESV notes that “princes” may mean “officials”). Those who seized others’ land to enlarge their borders will be driven out of their own.

God sees the unborn. God names the unborn as victims: their lives mattered to him. Every society that treats the weak and the unborn as obstacles to its ambitions stands under this word. The Son of God himself was once an unborn child, and the unborn John leapt for joy in his presence (Luke 1:41–44). Anyone who carries the grief or guilt of such a loss should hear the other word of Scripture too: in Christ there is full forgiveness and a welcome home (1 John 1:9).

The circle is closing. Picture the crowd in Israel cheering as each enemy is condemned. But Amos is drawing a circle around them, and in the next chapter it reaches Judah, and then Israel itself. Before we cheer at God’s judgment on others, we must remember that “all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23).

1.title: The Lion Roars
1.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 1 opens the book. A single verse introduces the shepherd from Tekoa and dates his words; then the theme of the whole book sounds at once, “The LORD roars from Zion” (v. 2), and the first five of eight judgment speeches follow, against the nations around Israel.

The message. The God of Israel is the Judge of all the earth, and no nation is beyond his reach. Peoples who never had his written law are still accountable for cruelty that every conscience knows is wrong: crushing the defenceless, trading human beings, breaking faith, nursing hatred, butchering the unborn for land. God is patient, but his patience has a measure, and when it is full he answers violence with the fire it lit.

Why it was said. Israel was prosperous, sure of God’s favour (see the introduction), and glad to hear its enemies condemned. Amos uses that gladness: each oracle draws the circle tighter around his hearers until, in chapter 2, it closes on them.

How the chapter makes its case. The heading sets the words in history: a herdsman, two kings, and an earthquake long remembered (v. 1). Then comes the roar that withers the land from the southern pastures to the top of Carmel (v. 2). Five oracles follow, each in the same pattern, “For three transgressions … and for four”, naming one representative crime and announcing fire. Damascus threshed Gilead with iron (vv. 3–5). Gaza sold whole communities to Edom (vv. 6–8), and Tyre did the same, breaking a covenant of brotherhood besides (vv. 9–10). Edom hunted his brother and kept his anger for ever (vv. 11–12). Ammon ripped open pregnant women to move a border (vv. 13–15).

Where it leads. Chiefly by the character of God revealed in Christ, and by the need the chapter exposes. The Lord who roars from Zion has come as “the Lion of the tribe of Judah”, yet when John turned to look he saw “a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain” (Revelation 5:5–6). The Judge of the nations has not lowered his standard; in his Son he has borne its sentence himself, and by that blood he ransoms people “from every tribe and language and people and nation” (Revelation 5:9), the descendants of these very nations among them.

For us. This chapter forbids two easy responses: shrugging at atrocities as somebody else’s culture, and enjoying God’s judgment on others as if it could never touch us. God sees the trafficked, the unborn and the victims of old grudges, and so must we. And the circle that closes in chapter 2 closes on every reader, which is why the only safe place is with the Lamb who was slain.
1.theology:
God speaks, and his word of judgment is like a lion's roar that no one can ignore (v. 2; 3:8; Joel 3:16; Rev 5:5).

God rules over all nations, not Israel only, and he is patient, but his patience has an end (vv. 3, 6, 9, 11, 13; Acts 17:30-31).

Even nations without the written law are accountable to God, because his law is written on the conscience and every person bears his image (vv. 3-15; Rom 1:18-20; 2:14-15; Gen 9:6).

God hates cruelty, trafficking, broken promises, lasting hatred and violence against the helpless, including the unborn, and he repays such sin with the same harm it did: nations that brought fire and exile on others will meet them themselves (vv. 3-15; Obad 15).

Judgment on others is a warning to ourselves, for all have sinned (vv. 3-15; 2:4-6; Rom 2:1; 3:23).
1.examples:
A shepherd from the south is sent to the palaces of the north, and his message begins with a lion's roar that withers the top of Carmel.

Then come iron sledges dragged over people as if they were grain, a brother who kept his anger forever, and unborn children killed for a few more miles of land, while Israel cheers, not seeing the circle of judgment closing around it.

keyVerse.quote: The LORD roars from Zion and utters his voice from Jerusalem; the pastures of the shepherds mourn, and the top of Carmel withers.
keyVerse.note: This verse announces the theme of the whole book: Israel’s God speaks in judgment, from the place he chose, and the whole land feels it. Everything that follows, against the nations and then against Israel, is this roar spelled out. In Christ the Lion of the tribe of Judah is also the Lamb who was slain, so the voice that judges is the voice that saves all who come to him.

1.reflection:
Amos condemns nations that never had God’s written law for cruelty that every conscience knows is wrong (vv. 3–15). What does this tell us about the moral sense in every human being? How would you answer someone who says morality is simply a matter of culture?

The sins named here include trafficking, broken promises, a grudge kept for generations and the killing of the unborn for gain. Which of them has a form in our own society, or in our own hearts?

Edom “kept his wrath forever” (v. 11). Is there an old grudge in your family, church or life that needs to be handed to God? What would it look like to forgive without pretending the wrong never happened?

Israel would have cheered as each enemy was condemned. Why is it so easy to enjoy God’s judgment on others, and how does seeing the Lion of Judah as the Lamb who was slain (Revelation 5:5–6) change the way we hear this chapter?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God defends the dignity even of an enemy of his people. Moab, east of the Dead Sea, had committed an outrage not against Israel but against Edom: it burned the bones of Edom’s king to lime, destroying him even after death (v. 1). Fire will fall on Kerioth, and Moab will die in the din of battle, amid shouting and the blast of the trumpet, its ruler and princes with it (vv. 2–3). Israel’s hearers might have expected God to care only for wrongs done to Israel. Instead he judges a wrong done to Israel’s old enemy, because every human being, friend or foe, living or dead, is made in his image.
verseByVerse.theology: God defends the dignity of every human being, even in death, and even an enemy of his people.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "For three transgressions of Moab, and for four, I will not revoke the punishment, because he burned to lime the bones of the king of Edom. So I will send a fire upon Moab, and it shall devour the strongholds of Kerioth, and Moab shall die amid uproar, amid shouting and the sound of the trumpet; I will cut off the ruler from its midst, and will kill all its princes with him," says the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moab desecrated the remains of an enemy king, and God, who guards the dignity of every human being, will bring Moab down in the noise of battle.

Burned to lime the bones of the king of Edom. Moab lay east of the Dead Sea. Its crime was not against Israel at all, but against Edom: perhaps digging up a dead king and burning his remains to powder. In the ancient world this was a terrible insult, an attempt to destroy a man even after death. When it happened we do not know.

Why this matters. Edom was no friend of Israel, yet God defends the dignity of its king. His justice is not favouritism toward his own side. Every human being, friend or enemy, living or dead, is made in his image and belongs to him.

The strongholds of Kerioth. Kerioth was a town of Moab. Moab will fall in the uproar of war, and its ruler and his “princes” (the ESV notes “officials”) will fall with it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Having God’s word brings no protection to those who reject it; it brings greater accountability. Now the circle reaches Amos’s own people, and the charge changes. The nations were condemned for cruelty that conscience condemns; Judah is condemned for despising the law of the LORD and refusing his statutes, led astray by the same lies, its idols, that had misled its fathers (v. 4). The fire that fell on the pagan cities will fall on Jerusalem too, the city of the temple (v. 5). Northern hearers would have enjoyed hearing their southern rival named, but the standard by which Judah is judged, God’s revealed word, is about to be applied to them.
verseByVerse.theology: Having God's word brings no protection to those who reject it.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "For three transgressions of Judah, and for four, I will not revoke the punishment, because they have rejected the law of the LORD, and have not kept his statutes, but their lies have led them astray, those after which their fathers walked. So I will send a fire upon Judah, and it shall devour the strongholds of Jerusalem."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah, which had God’s written word, is condemned for rejecting it, and even Jerusalem, the city of the temple, will burn.

They have rejected the law of the LORD. Israel would have enjoyed hearing its southern rival condemned. But the charge changes. The other nations were judged for cruelty that conscience condemns; Judah is judged for rejecting “the law of the LORD”. It had God’s written word, and more is expected from those who have it: “Everyone to whom much was given, of him much will be required” (Luke 12:48).

Their lies have led them astray. “Their lies” probably means false gods and false teaching, the empty idols that had deceived “their fathers” too. Sin had become a family tradition.

The strongholds of Jerusalem. Even the city of God’s temple is not safe. About 170 years later the Babylonians “burned the house of the LORD and the king’s house and all the houses of Jerusalem” (2 Kings 25:9). Being near God’s things is no substitute for obeying God’s word, and we, who have the whole of Scripture and the Word made flesh, have more to answer for than Judah.
verseByVerse.note: Judah is the only nation in chapters 1 and 2 charged with rejecting God's written law.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The greater God’s kindness to a people, the greater their guilt when they despise it. At last the circle closes on Israel, the people listening, and its charge sheet is the longest of all. Its sins are not war crimes against foreigners but injustice against its own neighbours: the innocent sold for debt, the poor trampled, a young woman used by father and son, and worship held on pawned cloaks with wine bought from fines (vv. 6–8). All this from a people God had rescued from Egypt, led through the wilderness and given a land, and to whom he gave prophets and Nazirites, whom they corrupted and silenced (vv. 9–12). So God will press them down, and no speed, strength or courage will save them (vv. 13–16).
verseByVerse.theology: The greater God's kindness to a people, the greater their guilt when they despise it.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "For three transgressions of Israel, and for four, I will not revoke the punishment, because they sell the righteous for silver, and the needy for a pair of sandals— those who trample the head of the poor into the dust of the earth and turn aside the way of the afflicted; a man and his father go in to the same girl, so that my holy name is profaned; they lay themselves down beside every altar on garments taken in pledge, and in the house of their God they drink the wine of those who have been fined.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel itself is guilty, not of atrocities against foreigners, but of crushing its own poor and then worshipping God with the proceeds.

For three transgressions of Israel. Now the trap springs, and the circle closes around the very people listening. It is like Nathan telling David about a rich man who stole a poor man’s lamb, and then saying, “You are the man!” (2 Samuel 12:7). And Israel’s charge sheet is by far the longest.

They sell the righteous for silver. “The righteous” here are the innocent, those in the right. They were sold into slavery for debt, or judges were bribed to condemn them. “The needy for a pair of sandals”: a poor man could lose his freedom over a debt as small as the price of a pair of shoes.

Those who trample the head of the poor. The rich trample the poor into the dust and push aside anyone who tries to get justice. Then comes sexual sin: “a man and his father go in to the same girl”. She may have been a servant girl in the household or a woman at a pagan shrine; either way, father and son use her, and God says his “holy name is profaned”, because his people bear his name. God sees the girl these men treated as nothing: her wrong is his concern.

On garments taken in pledge. A poor man who borrowed could give his cloak as security, and God’s law said, “you shall return it to him before the sun goes down, for that is his only covering” (Exodus 22:26–27). But the lenders kept the cloaks and lay on them at feasts beside the altar, and drank wine bought with fines squeezed out of the poor “in the house of their God”. Their worship was paid for by the very people God had told them to protect. “Whoever oppresses a poor man insults his Maker” (Proverbs 14:31).

A warning for churchgoers. These were not pagans but worshippers, which makes the passage searching. A Christian can attend faithfully and still exploit people during the week: paying workers unfairly, lending on crushing terms, or simply looking away from a neighbour in need. God reads our worship by the way we treat the weak: “if anyone has the world’s goods and sees his brother in need, yet closes his heart against him, how does God’s love abide in him?” (1 John 3:17).

Remembering grace. The cure is not grim effort but remembering what God has done for us (vv. 9–10), as his love, poured into our hearts by the Spirit (Romans 5:5), opens them to the weak. Where we have closed ours, there is mercy: Christ never once closed his, his righteousness covers us, and when we confess, God forgives (1 John 1:9).

verseByVerse.quote: "Yet it was I who destroyed the Amorite before them, whose height was like the height of the cedars and who was as strong as the oaks; I destroyed his fruit above and his roots beneath. Also it was I who brought you up out of the land of Egypt and led you forty years in the wilderness, to possess the land of the Amorite. And I raised up some of your sons for prophets, and some of your young men for Nazirites. Is it not indeed so, O people of Israel?" declares the LORD. "But you made the Nazirites drink wine, and commanded the prophets, saying, 'You shall not prophesy.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything Israel had was God’s gift, from the land to the prophets, and Israel answered his grace by corrupting the devout and silencing his word.

It was I who destroyed the Amorite. The Amorite stands for the peoples of Canaan, who seemed like giants to the spies (Numbers 13:32–33). God cut them down like a tree, “his fruit above and his roots beneath”. He brought Israel out of Egypt, led them forty years through the wilderness and gave them the land. The emphasis falls on “I”: everything they had was his gift, and placing this kindness straight after the charge (vv. 6–8) shows how ungrateful the sin was.

I raised up some of your sons for prophets. God also gave spiritual gifts. Prophets brought his word. Nazirites took a special vow of devotion that included refusing all wine (Numbers 6:3), and were living reminders of holiness. Israel pressured the Nazirites to break their vows and told the prophets to be quiet. Amos himself heard it: “never again prophesy at Bethel” (7:13). “Is it not indeed so?” God asks, and they have no answer.

They silenced the prophets, and then the Son. Stephen asked, “Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute?” (Acts 7:52). The pattern reached its climax when God sent his Son, and the tenants of the vineyard said, “This is the heir. Come, let us kill him” (Mark 12:7). Every age, and every heart, has its ways of telling God’s word to be quiet.

Was the destruction of the Amorites just? It was God’s judgment on peoples whose sin had ripened (Genesis 15:16; Leviticus 18:24–25), carried out through Israel at one moment in history. It gives no warrant for violence in God’s name today.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, I will press you down in your place, as a cart full of sheaves presses down. Flight shall perish from the swift, and the strong shall not retain his strength, nor shall the mighty save his life; he who handles the bow shall not stand, and he who is swift of foot shall not save himself, nor shall he who rides the horse save his life; and he who is stout of heart among the mighty shall flee away naked in that day," declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because Israel pressed down the poor, God will press Israel down, and no speed, strength or courage will save anyone on that day.

As a cart full of sheaves presses down. A cart loaded with harvested grain presses down with crushing weight. Israel had pressed down the poor; now God will press them down.

Flight shall perish from the swift. Runner, strong man, archer, horseman: no strength helps. The bravest will run away “naked”, throwing off armour and clothes to escape. Israel trusted its military success under Jeroboam, in vain.

The one way of escape. The only escape from God’s judgment is not running but taking refuge in the One who bore it. Jesus came “to proclaim good news to the poor” and “to set at liberty those who are oppressed” (Luke 4:18), and “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9). Those who have received such grace cannot go on crushing the poor. “How shall we escape if we neglect such a great salvation?” (Hebrews 2:3).

Uncertain wording. The verb translated “press you down” is rare, and its meaning is uncertain. Most take it as “press” or “crush”, the cart groaning under its load; others connect it with words meaning “split open” or “groan”, picturing the ground cracking beneath them, perhaps an echo of the earthquake (1:1). Either way, the picture is of a weight no one can escape.

2.title: You Are the Man
2.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 2 completes the round of eight oracles that began in 1:3. After Ammon come Moab and then, to the crowd’s delight, Judah; and then the circle closes on Israel itself, with the longest and sharpest charge of all.

The message. Israel is no better than the nations it despised, and because it had more light it is more guilty. God sees how a people treats its poor as clearly as he sees war crimes, and he counts injustice dressed up as worship an insult to his holy name. Everything Israel had, its land, its freedom, its prophets, was his gift, and it used his gifts to crush the weak and silence his word.

Why it was said. Israel was prosperous and devout, and sure that judgment was for other people (see the introduction). Amos lets his hearers agree with every verdict on their neighbours, and then applies the same justice to them.

How the chapter makes its case. Moab is condemned for desecrating the bones of Edom’s king, a crime against Israel’s old enemy (vv. 1–3). Judah, Amos’s own people, is judged by a new standard: not cruelty but rejecting the law of the LORD (vv. 4–5). Then Israel: the innocent sold, the poor trampled, a young woman abused, and worship held on pawned cloaks with wine bought from fines (vv. 6–8). God recounts his grace: the Amorite destroyed, the exodus, the wilderness, prophets and Nazirites raised up, whom Israel corrupted and silenced (vv. 9–12). So he will press them down, and no speed, strength or courage will save them (vv. 13–16).

Where it leads. By the need it exposes, and by pattern. Paul’s argument in Romans 1–3 moves the same way: first the Gentiles, then the people who had the law, “so that every mouth may be stopped, and the whole world may be held accountable to God” (Romans 3:19). That leaves one way out, the righteousness of God given through faith in Jesus Christ (Romans 3:21–22). And Israel’s silencing of the prophets reached its climax when God sent his Son, and the tenants said, “This is the heir. Come, let us kill him” (Mark 12:7). The Righteous One was himself sold for silver (Matthew 26:15), and bore the judgment no strength could escape.

For us. Nathan’s “You are the man!” comes to every reader of this chapter. God measures our worship by how we treat the weak: workers, borrowers, women, the poor at the door. The cure is not to try harder in our own strength but to remember the grace of Christ, who became poor for us, and to let it open our hands.
2.theology:
God defends the dignity of every person, even an enemy, even in death (v. 1; Gen 9:6).

Those who have God's word are judged by it, and privilege increases responsibility (vv. 4-5; Luke 12:48; Rom 2:1).

Injustice against the poor is sin against God, and religion practised on the backs of the poor is hateful to him (vv. 6-8; Exod 22:26-27; Prov 14:31; Jas 2:6).

God's past kindness makes ingratitude more serious, not less, and silencing his messengers is a long rebellion that reached its climax in the rejection of Christ (vv. 9-12; 7:12-13; Acts 7:52; Matt 23:37).

No human strength can escape God's judgment; the only refuge is Christ, who became poor for our sake (vv. 13-16; Luke 4:18; 2 Cor 8:9; Heb 2:3).
2.examples:
God takes the side of an enemy king whose bones were burned to powder, and a crowd applauds judgment until the prophet reaches their own nation.

Then the pictures come close to home: a man sold into slavery for the price of a pair of shoes, a poor man's only cloak spread out at a worship feast, a Nazirite handed a cup of wine, and the bravest soldier running from the battle without his clothes.

keyVerse.quote: For three transgressions of Israel, and for four, I will not revoke the punishment, because they sell the righteous for silver, and the needy for a pair of sandals
keyVerse.note: Here the trap springs: after condemning every neighbour, God names the people who were cheering. Their crime is not war on foreigners but the sale of their own poor, which shows that God measures a people first by how it treats the weak. It points to the Righteous One who was himself sold for silver, and who bore the judgment his people deserved.

2.reflection:
Amos’s hearers must have enjoyed the oracles against their enemies until the last one. Why do we find it easier to see sin in others than in ourselves? How does Nathan’s “You are the man!” (2 Samuel 12:7) help explain what Amos is doing?

Judah is judged for rejecting God’s word (v. 4), and Israel for silencing the prophets (v. 12). In what ways do Christians today tell God’s word to be quiet, in church or in their own hearts?

Israel’s worship was paid for by what it took from the poor (v. 8). Where might our comfort, spending or business depend on someone else’s hardship? What practical step could you take this month?

God reminds Israel of all he had done for them (vv. 9–11) before announcing judgment. How does remembering grace, above all the grace of Christ who became poor for us (2 Corinthians 8:9), change the way we treat the weak?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Being chosen by God is not a shield against judgment but the reason for greater accountability. God speaks to the whole family he brought out of Egypt and reminds them that he has “known” them, bound himself to them in love, as he has no other nation; therefore he will punish all their iniquities (vv. 1–2). Then come seven questions from country life, each with the obvious answer “No”: nothing happens without a cause, and disaster in a city comes from the LORD (vv. 3–6). Yet he does nothing without first revealing it to his prophets (v. 7). The lion has roared, so everyone should fear; God has spoken, so Amos must prophesy (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: Being chosen by God is not a shield against judgment but a reason for greater accountability.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear this word that the LORD has spoken against you, O people of Israel, against the whole family that I brought up out of the land of Egypt: "You only have I known of all the families of the earth; therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because God chose Israel and bound himself to it in love, he will hold it to account for every sin. Privilege does not cancel judgment; it deepens it.

Hear this word. The sermons to Israel begin (chapters 3–6). God addresses “the whole family” he brought out of Egypt, Judah included, and reminds them who they are: a family he redeemed.

You only have I known. God obviously knows about every nation; chapters 1–2 have just shown it. But in the Bible, for God to “know” someone often means to choose them and bind himself to them in love: “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you” (Jeremiah 1:5). Out of all the nations God set his love on Israel, not because they were great, but simply because he loved them (Deuteronomy 7:7–8).

Therefore I will punish you. We expect “therefore I will protect you”. Instead it is “therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities.” Israel thought being chosen meant they were safe however they lived. But the closer the relationship, the more serious the betrayal, as a husband’s unfaithfulness wounds as a stranger’s rudeness never could.

For the church today. Peter writes, “it is time for judgment to begin at the household of God” (1 Peter 4:17). God’s discipline of a Christian is not a sign that he has abandoned us but that he loves us: “the Lord disciplines the one he loves” (Hebrews 12:6). Grace is never a licence to sin; those who know they are loved will not treat that love lightly, and the Spirit who assures them of it (Romans 8:16) makes them holy.

The Son he knew. The Father’s beloved Son was known as no one else, and on the cross the iniquities of God’s chosen people were laid on him (Isaiah 53:6). So for those in Christ, discipline is never condemnation (Romans 8:1).

verseByVerse.quote: "Do two walk together, unless they have agreed to meet? Does a lion roar in the forest, when he has no prey? Does a young lion cry out from his den, if he has taken nothing? Does a bird fall in a snare on the earth, when there is no trap for it? Does a snare spring up from the ground, when it has taken nothing? Is a trumpet blown in a city, and the people are not afraid? Does disaster come to a city, unless the LORD has done it?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nothing happens without a cause: when disaster comes to a city, the LORD is behind it, and when a prophet speaks, it is because God has spoken.

Do two walk together, unless they have agreed to meet? A countryman’s questions, and every answer is plainly “No”: two do not meet in open country by chance, a lion does not roar over nothing, a trap does not spring without a catch. Israel wanted to know why this shepherd from Judah preached so harshly; the questions lead to the answer in verse 8: because God has spoken.

Is a trumpet blown in a city, and the people are not afraid? The watchman’s trumpet means an enemy is coming, and everyone trembles. Then the last question comes home: who is behind disaster? “The LORD has done it.” Israel’s disasters will not be accidents or mere politics.

Does God only allow disasters? Some Christians prefer to say that God only permits them. The Reformed tradition, following passages like this, teaches that God rules over all things, calamity included: “I make well-being and create calamity; I am the LORD, who does all these things” (Isaiah 45:7). Yet God is never the author of sin, and those who do evil are fully responsible for it. The comfort is great: no disaster is meaningless, nothing is outside the hand of a God who is wise and good, and nothing can snatch his people out of Christ’s hand (John 10:28).

What it does not mean. Not that every disaster is punishment for a particular sin of those it strikes (Luke 13:1–5; John 9:3). Amos interprets a judgment God announced in advance through his prophet; we have no such word about the troubles of our neighbours, and should never tell a grieving family why God sent their loss.

verseByVerse.quote: "For the Lord GOD does nothing without revealing his secret to his servants the prophets. The lion has roared; who will not fear? The Lord GOD has spoken; who can but prophesy?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God warns before he strikes, and when he has spoken, his prophet cannot keep silent.

His secret to his servants the prophets. God does not bring judgment without warning; he tells “his servants the prophets” first. A “secret” is something shared only with those close to you. Long before, God said of his friend Abraham, “Shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do” (Genesis 18:17). The very fact that Amos is preaching is a mercy: God warns so that people may turn.

The Lord GOD has spoken; who can but prophesy? Verse 8 brings together the lion of 1:2 and the questions of verses 3–6. As everyone fears a lion’s roar, so when God speaks the prophet cannot keep silent. Amos did not choose this ministry; he speaks because he must. Jeremiah felt the word as “a burning fire shut up in my bones” (Jeremiah 20:9), and the apostles said, “we cannot but speak of what we have seen and heard” (Acts 4:20).

What we have received. Jesus told his disciples, “all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15:15). In Scripture God has openly told us his plans; no one will say on the last day that he was not warned.

The preacher and the hearer. The preacher must speak, and every faithful pastor feels it: “Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel!” (1 Corinthians 9:16). The hearer should tremble, not with a panic that runs from God, but with the reverent fear that runs to him for mercy.

Are there prophets today who receive God’s secret plans? God has now spoken his final word in his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2), revealed in the Scriptures; no one today receives new revelation of his plans. Faithful Christians differ about whether lesser gifts of prophecy continue, but all who hold to a closed canon agree that nothing given today can add to Scripture or stand beside it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wealth stored up by violence, and worship that shelters it, will both fall on the day God acts. Heralds summon Ashdod and Egypt, pagan nations, to gather on the hills around Samaria and look at the turmoil and oppression inside it: its rulers no longer know how to do right, and their strongholds are full of plunder (vv. 9–10). So an enemy will surround the land and plunder the plunderers, and Israel will be “rescued” only as a shepherd rescues two legs or an ear from a lion, proof that the sheep is gone (vv. 11–12). God will punish the altars of Bethel, cutting off the horns where the guilty sought refuge, and bring down the winter houses, summer houses and ivory houses of the rich (vv. 13–15).
verseByVerse.theology: False worship and luxury built on injustice will both fall on the day God acts.

verseByVerse.quote: Proclaim to the strongholds in Ashdod and to the strongholds in the land of Egypt, and say, "Assemble yourselves on the mountains of Samaria, and see the great tumults within her, and the oppressed in her midst." "They do not know how to do right," declares the LORD, "those who store up violence and robbery in their strongholds."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even pagan nations are summoned to look at Samaria, because its rulers have filled their strongholds with what they took by violence.

Proclaim to the strongholds in Ashdod. God calls for witnesses, as in a courtroom, and chooses surprising ones: Ashdod, a Philistine city, and Egypt, Israel’s ancient oppressor, invited to gather on the hills around Samaria and look down into it. The nation God rescued from slavery in Egypt now enslaves its own people, and Egypt is called to see it.

They do not know how to do right. Samaria’s rulers had lost even that ability: sin practised long enough dulls the conscience until it no longer feels wrong. Their great houses were full of treasure, but God called it what it was, “violence and robbery”, wealth taken from the poor and stored away. James says the same to the rich who oppress: “their corrosion will be evidence against you” (James 5:3).

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: "An adversary shall surround the land and bring down your defenses from you, and your strongholds shall be plundered." Thus says the LORD: "As the shepherd rescues from the mouth of the lion two legs, or a piece of an ear, so shall the people of Israel who dwell in Samaria be rescued, with the corner of a couch and part of a bed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An enemy will plunder the plunderers, and all that will be left of Samaria’s rich is scraps, proof that they are gone.

Your strongholds shall be plundered. The punishment fits the crime: the strongholds where they stored up plunder will themselves be plundered. Amos does not name the enemy, but history does: Assyria besieged Samaria for three years and carried Israel into exile (2 Kings 17:5–6).

As the shepherd rescues from the mouth of the lion. If a wild animal killed a sheep in a shepherd’s care, he had to bring back what was left as evidence that he had not stolen it: “If it is torn by beasts, let him bring it as evidence” (Exodus 22:13). So a shepherd might pull “two legs, or a piece of an ear” from a lion’s mouth. That is not a rescue. It is proof that the sheep is dead.

The corner of a couch and part of a bed. Israel will be “rescued” in the same way. All that will be left of the rich in Samaria is a bit of the furniture they lounged on (6:4), evidence that they were ever there. Those who expect to come through the disaster with their comforts intact will find nothing but scraps.

The Shepherd who loses none. Amos’s shepherd could save only an ear. Christ went into the lion’s mouth himself: “The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep”, and of his sheep he says, “they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand” (John 10:11, 28).

Uncertain wording. In verse 11 the Hebrew is abrupt, and the ESV gives a more literal rendering in a note. In verse 12 the meaning of the word translated “part” is uncertain (also an ESV note). Its letters resemble the name Damascus, so some think of fabric or furniture from Damascus, others of “the leg” or “the back” of a bed. Either way, a fragment of luxury furniture is all that will be left.

verseByVerse.quote: "Hear, and testify against the house of Jacob," declares the Lord GOD, the God of hosts, "that on the day I punish Israel for his transgressions, I will punish the altars of Bethel, and the horns of the altar shall be cut off and fall to the ground. I will strike the winter house along with the summer house, and the houses of ivory shall perish, and the great houses shall come to an end," declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the day God punishes Israel, the false altars it trusted and the luxurious houses it built from oppression will fall together.

Hear, and testify. The foreign witnesses of verse 9 are addressed again by “the God of hosts”, commander of heaven’s armies, from whom no army could protect Israel.

The altars of Bethel. Bethel was the chief shrine of the northern kingdom, where Jeroboam I had set up a golden calf (1 Kings 12:28–29): the heart of Israel’s religion. Altars had “horns”, projections at each corner, and a person fleeing for his life could take hold of them to seek mercy (1 Kings 1:50). Cut off the horns, and no refuge is left. More than a century later King Josiah pulled down the altar at Bethel and burned it (2 Kings 23:15).

The one true altar. Only one altar truly offers refuge: Christ’s sacrifice, where sinners can take hold and find mercy. Hebrews speaks of believers “who have fled for refuge” to hold fast to the hope set before them (Hebrews 6:18).

The winter house along with the summer house. The wealthy had a winter house and a summer house (compare Jeremiah 36:22), and some had “houses of ivory”, decorated with carved ivory panels. King Ahab had built an “ivory house” in Samaria (1 Kings 22:39), and archaeologists there have found many pieces of carved ivory. “The great houses” (the ESV notes “many houses”) will come to an end.

Treasure on earth. God is not against homes or beautiful things, but these were built with what was taken from the poor, and trusted in. Jesus warned, “Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth … For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matthew 6:19, 21). Everything we build without God will come to an end; only what is built on Christ will last, for “we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ” (2 Corinthians 5:10).

3.title: You Only Have I Known
3.overview:
Where we are. With the eight oracles complete, Amos turns to Israel alone. Chapter 3 opens the sermons of chapters 3–6, three of which begin “Hear this word” (3:1; 4:1; 5:1), and it presses home the verdict of 2:6–16.

The message. Being chosen by God is not a shield against judgment but the reason for it. God bound himself to Israel in love as to no other nation, so its sins are a betrayal, and he will call it to account. He does not act without warning, and his prophet speaks because God has roared. The wealth Israel stored up by violence, and the altar it trusted, will not survive the day he acts.

Why it was said. Israel believed its election guaranteed its safety, and it resented a herdsman from Judah preaching doom at its shrines (see the introduction; 7:10–13). This chapter answers both.

How the chapter makes its case. God addresses the family he brought out of Egypt: “You only have I known … therefore I will punish you” (vv. 1–2). A chain of countryman’s questions shows that nothing happens without a cause: disaster in a city is the LORD’s doing, he reveals his plan to his prophets first, and when the lion roars the prophet must speak (vv. 3–8). Pagan Ashdod and Egypt are summoned to look down on Samaria’s oppression (vv. 9–10). An enemy will plunder its strongholds, and only scraps will be “rescued”, like the remains of a sheep pulled from a lion’s mouth (vv. 11–12). God will cut off the horns of Bethel’s altar and bring down the winter houses, summer houses and ivory houses of the rich (vv. 13–15).

Where it leads. By covenant, and by the character of God revealed in Christ. The God who “knew” Israel has now made himself known in his Son, and his people’s privilege and accountability are greater: “it is time for judgment to begin at the household of God” (1 Peter 4:17). Yet the judgment due to God’s household fell first on the Son he knew and loved, who bore his people’s iniquities. Amos’s shepherd could rescue only two legs or an ear; the good shepherd “lays down his life for the sheep” and loses none of them (John 10:11, 28). And when the horns of every false altar are cut off, one refuge remains: the cross.

For us. Church membership, a Christian upbringing and sound doctrine are great privileges, but they are not a shield; they make us more accountable. Listen when God speaks in his word, for he warns before he acts. And hold your possessions loosely: only what is built on Christ will last.
3.theology:
God's choice of his people is an act of free love, and it brings greater accountability, not immunity from judgment (vv. 1-2; Deut 7:6-8; Luke 12:48; 1 Pet 4:17; Heb 12:6).

God rules over all events, including calamity, yet he is never the author of sin (v. 6; Isa 45:7; Lam 3:37-38).

God warns before he judges, revealing his purposes through his prophets and finally through his Son; when he speaks, hearers should fear and his messengers cannot keep silent (vv. 7-8; Gen 18:17; Heb 1:1-2; John 15:15; Jer 20:9; Acts 4:20; 1 Cor 9:16).

Wealth gained by oppression is stored-up guilt, and it will not last (vv. 9-10, 15; Jas 5:1-3; Matt 6:19-21).

False worship offers no refuge; the only true place of mercy is the sacrifice of Christ (v. 14; 1 Kgs 1:50; 2 Cor 5:10).
3.examples:
A chosen family is told that its privilege makes its guilt heavier, and a shepherd's questions about lions and traps show that nothing happens without a cause, while the prophet cannot keep God's word shut up inside him.

Then Egypt and the Philistines are invited to sit on the hills and watch Samaria's injustice, a shepherd holds up two legs and a piece of an ear, and an altar loses its horns, leaving no refuge but the one Christ provides.

keyVerse.quote: You only have I known of all the families of the earth; therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities.
keyVerse.note: This verse overturns Israel’s confidence in a single word: “therefore”. Being chosen and loved by God did not make Israel safe in its sin; it made the sin a betrayal and the judgment certain. It speaks to every church and every believer, and it sends us to the Son the Father knew and loved, on whom the iniquities of his people were laid.

3.reflection:
“You only have I known … therefore I will punish you” (v. 2). Why does being chosen and loved by God make sin more serious, not less? What privileges might we be tempted to treat as a shield?

Amos says disaster does not come to a city “unless the LORD has done it” (v. 6). How does God’s rule over hard things comfort you? Why must we be careful never to tell suffering people why God sent their trouble?

Amos could not keep silent once God had spoken (v. 8). Is there a truth from God’s word that you keep quiet about in your family, workplace or church because saying it would be costly?

The rich of Samaria trusted their houses and their altar (vv. 13–15). What do people around us trust for safety? What does it mean in practice to take hold of Christ as our only refuge?
