verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Cows of Bashan and Busy Worshippers
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Luxury built on oppression and worship that loves to be seen are both hateful to God. Amos addresses the wealthy women of Samaria as “cows of Bashan”, fat on the good life, whose demands for drink drive their husbands to crush the poor (v. 1). God swears by his own holiness that they will be hauled away like fish on hooks and marched out through the breaches in the broken walls (vv. 2–3). Then, sounding like a priest calling worshippers, Amos invites Israel to Bethel and Gilgal to sin and sin again, with daily sacrifices, constant tithes and loudly advertised offerings (vv. 4–5). Their worship is zealous, generous and public, and it is all for themselves.
verseByVerse.theology: Luxury built on oppression and worship that loves to be seen are both hateful to God.

verseByVerse.quote: "Hear this word, you cows of Bashan, who are on the mountain of Samaria, who oppress the poor, who crush the needy, who say to your husbands, 'Bring, that we may drink!' The Lord GOD has sworn by his holiness that, behold, the days are coming upon you, when they shall take you away with hooks, even the last of you with fishhooks. And you shall go out through the breaches, each one straight ahead; and you shall be cast out into Harmon," declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The pampered women of Samaria, whose comfort is paid for by crushing the poor, will be dragged into exile, for God counts them among the oppressors.

You cows of Bashan. Bashan was rich grazing land east of the Jordan, famous for its sleek, well-fed cattle (Deuteronomy 32:14). Amos calls the wealthy women of Samaria “cows of Bashan”, a shocking insult from a man who worked with animals. They may never have struck a poor person themselves, but their demands drove the system: “Bring, that we may drink!” Their husbands squeezed the poor to pay for their wives’ parties, and God counts the wives among those “who oppress the poor”.

Sworn by his holiness. God swears “by his holiness”, because there is nothing higher to swear by. Those who lived like fattened cattle will be dragged away like fish on hooks and marched out single file through the gaps (“the breaches”), each one “straight ahead”, and cast out towards Harmon.

A warning for the comfortable. We may never cheat anyone, yet happily enjoy the fruits of injustice without asking where they came from. Scripture charges the rich “not to be haughty, nor to set their hopes on the uncertainty of riches, but on God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy” (1 Timothy 6:17).

The Lord who served. The women of Samaria said, “Bring, that we may drink!” The Lord of glory, who on the cross said “I thirst” (John 19:28), came “not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45).

Uncertain wording. The words translated “hooks” and “fishhooks” are uncertain; they may mean hooks, thorns, or baskets in which a catch is carried away. Assyrian carvings show captives led by cords through the lip or nose, and God speaks of putting his hook in an enemy’s nose (2 Kings 19:28), so the ESV’s picture is likely. Harmon is unknown: perhaps a place on the road into exile, though some read it as Mount Hermon to the north. The meaning is plain: no one will escape.
verseByVerse.note: Psalm 22:12 also uses the strong bulls of Bashan as a picture of proud, hostile power.

verseByVerse.quote: "Come to Bethel, and transgress; to Gilgal, and multiply transgression; bring your sacrifices every morning, your tithes every three days; offer a sacrifice of thanksgiving of that which is leavened, and proclaim freewill offerings, publish them; for so you love to do, O people of Israel!" declares the Lord GOD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel’s busy, generous worship only adds to its sin, because those who offer it love religion and being seen, but not God or their neighbours.

Come to Bethel, and transgress. Heavy sarcasm: Amos sounds like a priest calling people to worship, but says, “Come to Bethel, and transgress; to Gilgal, and multiply transgression.” Every visit to Israel’s great shrines only added to their sin: the more zealous they were in religion while oppressing the poor, the guiltier they became.

Your tithes every three days. The details are mock-generous. The law asked for tithes once a year, with a special tithe for the poor every third year (Deuteronomy 14:22–29), and Amos pictures them tithing “every three days”. Leaven was not to be burned on the altar (Leviticus 2:11), yet they make a show of offering “that which is leavened”. Their eagerness ran past what God had asked, and away from what he cared about.

For so you love to do. The last words show the heart of it. They loved religion. They loved to “proclaim” and “publish” their offerings so that everyone knew. But they did not love God, and they did not love their neighbours. Jesus described the same thing: hypocrites who “love to stand and pray … that they may be seen by others” (Matthew 6:5). It is possible to be very religious and very far from God.

The worship God seeks. The only offering that ever fully pleased God was his Son’s, made not for display but in agony and shame. Those who trust it need not perform for God or for anyone else; they bring their gifts quietly to the Father “who sees in secret” (Matthew 6:4). Ask what you would still give, and how you would still worship, if no one ever knew.
verseByVerse.note: Gilgal was where Israel first camped in the land and set up twelve memorial stones (Josh 4:19-20).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–13 — Yet You Did Not Return to Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s hard providences are calls to repentance, and those who refuse every call must at last meet God himself. Five times God recalls what he sent, and five times the same lament follows: “yet you did not return to me”. He sent famine, so that teeth had nothing to chew (v. 6); drought, falling on one town and not the next (vv. 7–8); blight, mildew and locusts (v. 9); plague and defeat in war (v. 10); and an overthrow like Sodom’s, from which Israel was snatched like a burning stick (v. 11). So God will come himself: “prepare to meet your God” (v. 12). A hymn tells who that is: the Creator of mountains and wind, who turns dawn to darkness and treads the heights (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: God's hard providences are calls to repentance, and those who refuse them must at last meet God himself.

verseByVerse.quote: "I gave you cleanness of teeth in all your cities, and lack of bread in all your places, yet you did not return to me," declares the LORD. "I also withheld the rain from you when there were yet three months to the harvest; I would send rain on one city, and send no rain on another city; one field would have rain, and the field on which it did not rain would wither; so two or three cities would wander to another city to drink water, and would not be satisfied; yet you did not return to me," declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God had already sent famine and drought to call Israel home, and each time it refused to come.

Cleanness of teeth. Nothing to chew. God reviews disasters he had already sent, and they were not random: “I gave you”. His law had warned that if Israel broke the covenant, he would send famine, drought, disease and defeat (Deuteronomy 28:22–24). Each was a warning shot, meant to turn them back.

Yet you did not return to me. Five times the same sad refrain sounds (vv. 6, 8, 9, 10, 11). It is a father calling a wayward child home, again and again.

I also withheld the rain from you. The rain failed at the worst possible time, three months before harvest, when crops needed it most. And it fell in a strange pattern: one town had rain and the next did not, a sign that this was not mere weather but God showing his hand. Thirsty people staggered from town to town looking for water and “would not be satisfied”, yet they did not come to the One who gives living water (John 4:13–14).

verseByVerse.quote: "I struck you with blight and mildew; your many gardens and your vineyards, your fig trees and your olive trees the locust devoured; yet you did not return to me," declares the LORD. "I sent among you a pestilence after the manner of Egypt; I killed your young men with the sword, and carried away your horses, and I made the stench of your camp go up into your nostrils; yet you did not return to me," declares the LORD. "I overthrew some of you, as when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, and you were as a brand plucked out of the burning; yet you did not return to me," declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blight, locusts, plague, war and a near-destruction like Sodom’s all failed to bring Israel back, for suffering alone cannot change a hard heart.

Blight and mildew. Crops rotted with blight and mildew, and locusts ate the rest. Then came plague “after the manner of Egypt”: the plagues God once sent on Pharaoh were now falling on his own people, because they had become like Egypt. War killed their young men and captured their horses (the ESV notes the Hebrew reads “along with the captivity of your horses”), and the stench of unburied bodies filled the camp.

A brand plucked out of the burning. Some disaster, perhaps an earthquake or a great fire, could only be compared with the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 19:24–25). Israel survived it barely, like a burning stick snatched from the fire before it was consumed. Surely now they would turn back to God? Still they did not return.

Suffering and repentance. Suffering does not automatically make people repent. It can soften the heart, or it can harden it: Revelation describes people who lived through terrible plagues and still “did not repent of the works of their hands” (Revelation 9:20). God’s kindness and his discipline are both meant to lead us to repentance (Romans 2:4). When hardship comes, the right question is not only “Why me?” but “Lord, what are you calling me to turn from?” Yet not every hardship is the punishment of a particular sin (John 9:3), and for those in Christ it is a Father’s training, never his condemnation (Romans 8:1).

Would a loving God use pain to get our attention? To many today it sounds manipulative. We would rather treat famine and plague as pure accident. But if disasters mean nothing, they also say nothing, and we are left to suffer them in silence. C. S. Lewis, in The Problem of Pain, put the other view memorably: “God whispers to us in our pleasures, speaks in our conscience, but shouts in our pains: it is His megaphone to rouse a deaf world.” Amos records something sadder still: Israel heard the shout five times and turned over in bed. The deepest problem is not that God speaks too harshly but that we are so hard to wake. And the God who kept calling did not stay at a distance, shouting. In Christ he came into our hunger and grief himself, and on the cross took the worst of the judgment they warn of, so that for those who come home to him even pain becomes a Father’s voice.
verseByVerse.note: Zechariah 3:2 uses the same picture for Joshua the high priest, rescued by God's mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore thus I will do to you, O Israel; because I will do this to you, prepare to meet your God, O Israel!" For behold, he who forms the mountains and creates the wind, and declares to man what is his thought, who makes the morning darkness, and treads on the heights of the earth— the LORD, the God of hosts, is his name!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since every warning has failed, God will come himself, and Israel must prepare to meet the almighty Creator.

Prepare to meet your God, O Israel! After five warnings ignored, God sends no more warnings; he comes himself. He does not say what he will do, and the silence is more frightening than any description. The words echo Sinai, where Israel was told to be ready and was brought out “to meet God” (Exodus 19:15–17). Israel had been meeting at Bethel and Gilgal for worship; now they will meet God in judgment.

He who forms the mountains. Amos breaks into the first of three hymns (5:8–9; 9:5–6). He “forms the mountains” and “creates the wind”, the solid and the invisible alike. He “makes the morning darkness”, able to turn dawn into night. He “treads on the heights of the earth”, like a giant striding over the mountains. And he “declares to man what is his thought” (see the box below).

The God they had shrunk. Israel had shrunk God to a local god kept happy with sacrifices at Bethel; Amos lifts their eyes to the Creator of all things, whom no one can escape meeting.

Meeting God ourselves. These words are true for every person: “it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment” (Hebrews 9:27). How can anyone be ready? Not by religious activity like Israel’s, but by coming through Jesus Christ, who met God’s judgment in our place. The God who treads the heights of the earth came down to us. The prodigal son prepared to meet his father by coming home in repentance, and found his father running to embrace him (Luke 15:20). “Behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 6:2).

Uncertain wording. “Declares to man what is his thought” is ambiguous: “his” may be God’s, so that God reveals his own plans to people (3:7), or the man’s, so that God shows people their own hidden thoughts, since he knows them all (Psalm 139:2). Both are true of the God Israel must meet.

4.title: Prepare to Meet Your God
4.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 4 is the second of the sermons that open “Hear this word” (3:1; 4:1; 5:1). After the altars and ivory houses of 3:13–15, Amos turns to the women of Samaria, to the crowded shrines, and to a history of warnings Israel had ignored.

The message. Israel was busy with religion and deaf to God. It worshipped zealously and for show while crushing the poor, and it shrugged off every hardship God sent to call it home. So God will stop sending messages and come himself: “prepare to meet your God”. And the God they must meet is the Creator of the mountains and the wind.

Why it was said. Israel had come through years of hardship and defeat into prosperity (see the introduction) without asking what the hard years meant. Its shrines at Bethel and Gilgal were thriving, and it assumed God was pleased.

How the chapter makes its case. The pampered women of Samaria, whose demand for drink is paid for by crushing the needy, will be dragged out through the broken walls like fish on hooks (vv. 1–3). With biting irony Amos invites Israel to its shrines to “transgress” and “multiply transgression”, piling up sacrifices and advertising its gifts, because that is what it loves (vv. 4–5). Then God recounts the disasters he sent: famine, drought, blight and locust, plague and war, and an overthrow like Sodom’s; after each comes the same lament, “yet you did not return to me” (vv. 6–11). So Israel must prepare to meet its God, and a hymn tells who he is (vv. 12–13).

Where it leads. By the need it exposes, and by the character of God revealed in Christ. Five calls, five refusals: Israel’s problem was not lack of warning but a heart that would not turn, and no hardship could change it. Only God himself can meet that need, and he promised to give “a new heart” (Ezekiel 36:26). The summons “prepare to meet your God” has also been answered from God’s side. The Creator who “treads on the heights of the earth” came down to meet us in Jesus, bore the judgment that meeting would have brought, and turned it into a homecoming, like the father who ran to his returning son (Luke 15:20).

For us. Ask whether your religion is for God or for being seen, and whether it changes how you treat the poor. When hardship comes, ask what God may be calling you to turn from, without assuming every trouble is a punishment. Above all, prepare to meet God the only way anyone can: by coming home to him through Christ, today.
4.theology:
Enjoying luxury built on the oppression of the poor makes us guilty of that oppression (vv. 1-3; 1 Tim 6:17; Jas 5:1-3).

Religious zeal that loves display and ignores obedience multiplies sin rather than removing it (vv. 4-5; Matt 6:5).

God rules over famine, drought, disease and disaster, and uses them to call his people to return, yet suffering does not by itself produce repentance; hearts can harden under discipline (vv. 6-11; Deut 28:22-24; Lev 26:23-24; Rom 2:4; Rev 9:20-21; Jer 5:3).

Every person must meet God, and the only preparation is repentance and faith in Christ (v. 12; Heb 9:27; 2 Cor 6:2; Luke 15:17-20).

The God we must meet is the almighty Creator, whose name is the LORD of hosts (v. 13; Mic 1:3; Ps 139:1-4; Heb 10:31).
4.examples:
Pampered women call for another drink while the poor go hungry, and worshippers announce their generous offerings for all to hear.

Rain falls on one town and passes over the next, and a burning stick is pulled from the fire just in time.

keyVerse.quote: Therefore thus I will do to you, O Israel; because I will do this to you, prepare to meet your God, O Israel!
keyVerse.note: After five calls to return had been refused, God stops sending warnings and announces that he will come himself. The verse gathers up the whole chapter: religion without repentance cannot stand before the living God. Yet in the gospel God has come to meet us first, in his Son, so that all who come home through Christ can meet him without fear.

4.reflection:
The women of Samaria may never have struck a poor person, yet God counts them among the oppressors (v. 1). How might we enjoy the fruits of injustice without asking where they came from? What would it look like to start asking?

Israel’s worship was frequent, generous and public, “for so you love to do” (v. 5). How can we tell whether we love God or simply love religion and being seen? What helps keep our giving and worship for God alone?

Five times God says, “yet you did not return to me” (vv. 6–11). Why does hardship harden some people and soften others? When have hard times drawn you closer to God, and what made the difference?

“Prepare to meet your God” (v. 12) sounds like a threat. How does the gospel, in which God came down to meet us in Christ, change what it means to be ready to meet him?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Even over a nation already mourned as dead, God still holds out life to anyone who will seek him. Amos begins with a funeral song: virgin Israel has fallen, and its armies will come home with one man in ten (vv. 1–3). Then God speaks: seek me and live, but do not seek the famous shrines, for Bethel and Gilgal will go the way of their worshippers (vv. 4–6), people who have turned justice into something bitter (v. 7). At the centre of the chapter Amos sings of who this God is: the Maker of the stars, Lord of day, night and sea, who brings sudden ruin on the strongest fortress (vv. 8–9). He cannot be kept in a shrine, and he cannot be ignored.
verseByVerse.theology: Even as judgment approaches, God holds out life to all who will seek him, not religious places but himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear this word that I take up over you in lamentation, O house of Israel: "Fallen, no more to rise, is the virgin Israel; forsaken on her land, with none to raise her up." For thus says the Lord GOD: "The city that went out a thousand shall have a hundred left, and that which went out a hundred shall have ten left to the house of Israel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Amos sings a funeral song over a nation that is still alive, because in God’s sight Israel is already dead.

I take up over you in lamentation. A lamentation was a funeral song, sung over the dead, and verse 2 has the limping beat of one: a long line answered by a shorter one, as if the voice breaks. Imagine singing a dirge in a busy, prosperous city over people eating, trading and worshipping around you. That is what Amos did. And the lament is God’s own word: the Judge mourns those he must judge, for he has “no pleasure in the death of the wicked” (Ezekiel 33:11), which is why the funeral song is followed at once by an invitation (v. 4).

The virgin Israel. Israel is pictured as a young woman who should have had her whole life ahead of her, struck down and lying alone on the ground. “No more to rise”, “with none to raise her up”: no ally, no army and no idol will help. The northern kingdom did fall to Assyria and never rose again as a nation.

A hundred shall have ten left. Nine out of every ten fighting men would be lost. Behind the numbers are families waiting at the gate for sons who never come home. Yet even here a few are left, the first hint of the remnant of verse 15.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the LORD to the house of Israel: "Seek me and live; but do not seek Bethel, and do not enter into Gilgal or cross over to Beersheba; for Gilgal shall surely go into exile, and Bethel shall come to nothing." Seek the LORD and live, lest he break out like fire in the house of Joseph, and it devour, with none to quench it for Bethel, O you who turn justice to wormwood and cast down righteousness to the earth!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even after the funeral song, God offers life: seek me, not the famous shrines, and live.

Seek me and live. The sentence of death has been pronounced, and yet the Judge who has just sung Israel’s funeral song holds out life to the one he has mourned. This is the gospel in a single sentence. As long as the door is open, he calls. Isaiah says the same: “Seek the LORD while he may be found” (Isaiah 55:6).

Do not seek Bethel. Israel thought it was seeking God, and crowded into the famous holy places. Bethel was where God had met Jacob; Gilgal was where Israel first camped in the promised land; and Beersheba, in the far south of Judah, was where Abraham “called there on the name of the LORD” (Genesis 21:33). Pilgrims from the north even crossed the border into Judah to visit it. But a shrine with a great history cannot save anyone; Gilgal will go into exile and Bethel will come to nothing.

The house of Joseph. The northern kingdom, whose leading tribes, Ephraim and Manasseh, descended from Joseph. If they will not seek God, his judgment will break out like fire, and no priest at Bethel will be able to put it out.

Turn justice to wormwood. Wormwood is a very bitter plant (the ESV notes it may be “bitter fruit”). Justice should be sweet and life-giving to the poor; Israel’s courts had made it bitter, and righteousness was thrown to the ground and trampled. Seeking God and doing justice cannot be separated.

Not the place, but God. It is possible to love the church building, the tradition, the famous preacher or the religious experience, and never seek God himself. Jesus is not one holy place among many. He is “the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

How do I seek the LORD? Not by wandering about in search of a feeling, but by turning toward a Person who has spoken. Go where he has promised to be found. Not a shrine, but his word, prayer and his people gathered on the Lord’s Day. Open the Bible before you open the news, and read it to meet him, not only to finish a chapter. Seek him for himself. Notice when you want God mainly for what he can fix: the diagnosis, the exam, the job offer. Bring those, but ask for him too: “You will seek me and find me, when you seek me with all your heart” (Jeremiah 29:13). Leave the Bethels. Name whatever you have been running to instead, the habit, the reputation, the comfort you reach for at 2 a.m., and turn from it. Keep at it. Seeking is daily, not a single pilgrimage. And take heart: you are not the first seeker here. “For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost” (Luke 19:10). We seek him because he first came looking for us, and whoever comes to the Father through Christ finds the door already open.
verseByVerse.note: A pun in Hebrew: “Gilgal shall surely go into exile” (haggilgal galoh yigleh).

verseByVerse.quote: He who made the Pleiades and Orion, and turns deep darkness into the morning and darkens the day into night, who calls for the waters of the sea and pours them out on the surface of the earth, the LORD is his name; who makes destruction flash forth against the strong, so that destruction comes upon the fortress.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God Israel treated as a shrine-god is the Maker of the stars and the Lord of day, night and sea, and he can bring sudden ruin on the strongest fortress.

He who made the Pleiades and Orion. Once again Amos breaks into a hymn (compare 4:13). The Pleiades, a small cluster of stars, and Orion, the great hunter of the night sky, were familiar to every shepherd who watched his flock at night (Job 9:9). God made them. He controls day and night. He “calls for the waters of the sea”, drawing them up as clouds and pouring them out as rain, or perhaps as a flood. “The LORD is his name.”

Who makes destruction flash forth against the strong. The powerful thought their wealth and walls made them safe. God’s judgment strikes like lightning, suddenly and without warning, on the strong and on the fortress. That is why a hymn about the stars stands in a sermon about justice: the God who orders the heavens sees the courts of Samaria, and no bribe in the gate is hidden from him.

Darkness into morning. “Deep darkness” is the word behind “the shadow of death” in Psalm 23:4. The God who turns it into morning did so “on the first day of the week, at early dawn” (Luke 24:1), at an empty tomb, and he can turn a lost life into a new day.

Uncertain wording. The verb translated “makes … flash forth” in verse 9 is rare, and its exact sense is uncertain; some scholars even find more names of stars hidden in the verse. The ESV’s reading, God bringing sudden destruction on the strong, fits the context well, and the point is clear either way: the Creator is also the Judge.
verseByVerse.note: The same two constellations are named together in Job 9:9 and 38:31.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Seeking God shows itself in loving what he loves, above all in fair dealing with the weak. Israel’s powerful hate the honest voice in the court, squeeze the poor for grain, take bribes and send the needy away, so the stone houses and fine vineyards they built will never be theirs to enjoy (vv. 10–13). Again the call comes: seek good and not evil, hate evil, love good and set justice back up in the gate, and it may be that God will be gracious to a remnant (vv. 14–15). If not, he will pass through Israel as he once passed through Egypt, and mourning will fill every square, street and vineyard (vv. 16–17).
verseByVerse.theology: True seeking of God shows itself in loving what he loves and doing justice.

verseByVerse.quote: They hate him who reproves in the gate, and they abhor him who speaks the truth. Therefore because you trample on the poor and you exact taxes of grain from him, you have built houses of hewn stone, but you shall not dwell in them; you have planted pleasant vineyards, but you shall not drink their wine. For I know how many are your transgressions and how great are your sins— you who afflict the righteous, who take a bribe, and turn aside the needy in the gate. Therefore he who is prudent will keep silent in such a time, for it is an evil time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel’s powerful hate anyone who speaks up for justice in court and grow rich by squeezing the poor; God sees every bribe, and what they built by injustice they will never enjoy.

Him who reproves in the gate. In ancient Israel the town gate was the law court, where the elders sat to hear cases (Ruth 4:1). The one who “reproves in the gate” was the honest witness or judge who spoke up for what was right, and Israel’s leaders hated him. People who love sin always hate the one who exposes it, and Amos himself felt that hatred (7:10–13).

Houses of hewn stone. The rich trample on the poor and take their grain, and with the profits they build houses of cut stone instead of ordinary mud brick, and plant fine vineyards. But they will never enjoy them. God’s law had warned: “You shall build a house, but you shall not dwell in it. You shall plant a vineyard, but you shall not enjoy its fruit” (Deuteronomy 28:30). What is gained by injustice will be lost.

I know how many are your transgressions. The officials may have thought no one knew about the bribes. God says, “I know”: how many sins and how great. The righteous man is harassed, the judge takes a bribe, and the poor man who comes to court for help is sent away without a hearing.

The hated witness. Jesus said, “The world cannot hate you, but it hates me because I testify about it that its works are evil” (John 7:7). Condemned by a court that went looking for false witnesses, he bore that injustice to save the unjust, and his people will sometimes be the unwelcome voice in the gate.

He who is prudent will keep silent. Most likely a sad description of the times: things were so corrupt that sensible people kept quiet, because speaking up was useless or dangerous. It is not a command for believers to stay silent about injustice; Amos himself refused to.

Uncertain wording. The verb translated “trample” in verse 11 occurs only here, and its meaning is uncertain; the ESV notes that it may mean “you tax”, which fits the taxes of grain that follow. Verse 13 is also unclear: it may describe the wise keeping quiet because protest is useless (the commonest view), the wise falling silent before God when judgment comes, or the one who prospers keeping quiet to protect himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Seek good, and not evil, that you may live; and so the LORD, the God of hosts, will be with you, as you have said. Hate evil, and love good, and establish justice in the gate; it may be that the LORD, the God of hosts, will be gracious to the remnant of Joseph.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To seek God is to seek what he loves: hate evil, love good, and set justice back up in the courts; then, perhaps, God will be gracious to a remnant.

Seek good, and not evil. The call to seek and live comes a third time (vv. 4, 6, 14), and now it becomes practical. “As you have said”: Israel liked to say that God was with them. He truly will be, but only if they turn from evil. God’s presence is not a slogan for people who ignore his will.

Hate evil, and love good. Repentance is more than feeling sorry. It reaches the heart (“Hate evil, and love good”) and public life (“establish justice in the gate”). No one can make himself love good by decision; it is the work of the Spirit, who writes God’s law on the heart (Ezekiel 36:26–27). And no one has sought good perfectly, except Christ, in our place; his righteousness is credited to all who seek God through him (Philippians 3:9).

It may be that the LORD … will be gracious. Amos does not say God owes them mercy. Joel uses similar words: “Who knows whether he will not turn and relent” (Joel 2:14). Grace is always a gift, never something we can demand. Amos already sees that judgment will come, but “the remnant of Joseph”, a surviving few, may yet be spared, a hope that grows into the promise at the end of the book (9:8–15).

What this looks like. Amos’s three verbs reach our feelings, our tastes and the places where we have influence. Hate evil. Stop laughing along with what God calls cruel or unclean, whether in the office joke, the group chat or the evening’s entertainment; what we enjoy watching slowly shapes what we can no longer hate. Love good. Feed your affections on what is good: “Abhor what is evil; hold fast to what is good” (Romans 12:9). Notice and thank the honest colleague, the faithful carer, the kind neighbour. Establish justice in the gate. Yours may be a hiring panel, a school governors’ meeting, a church committee or a flat you let. Ask there who has no voice, and make sure they are heard and treated fairly, even when it costs you. None of this earns God’s favour. Christ “gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for himself a people for his own possession who are zealous for good works” (Titus 2:14). He has bought us out of evil, and his Spirit teaches our hearts to love what he loves.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the LORD, the God of hosts, the Lord: "In all the squares there shall be wailing, and in all the streets they shall say, 'Alas! Alas!' They shall call the farmers to mourning and to wailing those who are skilled in lamentation, and in all vineyards there shall be wailing, for I will pass through your midst," says the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because Israel will not seek him, God will pass through the land in judgment, and every street, square and vineyard will ring with mourning.

In all the squares there shall be wailing. The funeral song of verse 1 becomes a national funeral. There would be so many dead that even the farmers would be called from the fields to mourn beside “those who are skilled in lamentation”, the professional mourners hired for funerals (Jeremiah 9:17). Even the vineyards, places of song at harvest, will be filled with wailing.

I will pass through your midst. These words recall the Passover night, when God said, “I will pass through the land of Egypt that night” (Exodus 12:12). Then he passed through Egypt to judge it and spared his people. Now Israel has become like Egypt, and he will pass through them in judgment. Belonging to God’s people outwardly is no protection; then and now the only shelter is the blood of the lamb: “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7).

parallels.desc: the LORD passes through, now against Israel

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–27 — The Day of the LORD and the Feasts God Hates
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God refuses worship that is cut off from justice, and those who presume on his favour will find his day dark. Israel longed for the day of the LORD as its day of victory, but it will be darkness with no escape, like a man who flees a lion, meets a bear and is bitten by a snake at home (vv. 18–20). God hates their feasts, offerings and songs; what he wants is justice rolling down like waters and righteousness like a stream that never dries (vv. 21–24). Their worship had long been mixed with other gods, and the star-gods they made will go with them into exile beyond Damascus (vv. 25–27).
verseByVerse.theology: God refuses worship that is separated from justice, and those who presume on his day will find it dark.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to you who desire the day of the LORD! Why would you have the day of the LORD? It is darkness, and not light, as if a man fled from a lion, and a bear met him, or went into the house and leaned his hand against the wall, and a serpent bit him. Is not the day of the LORD darkness, and not light, and gloom with no brightness in it?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The day of the LORD that Israel longed for as its day of triumph will be a day of darkness for them, with no way of escape.

Woe to you who desire the day of the LORD! The day of the LORD was a popular hope in Israel: the day when God would defeat Israel’s enemies and bless his people. Amos says, “Woe to you.” They had forgotten that God’s day brings judgment on all sin, including theirs. For people living in rebellion it will be “darkness, and not light”.

As if a man fled from a lion. A picture any shepherd would understand. A man escapes a lion, only to run into a bear. He escapes the bear, gets safely home, leans against the wall to catch his breath, and a snake hidden in a crack bites him. Just when he feels safe, he is struck. So it will be on that day for those who are not right with God.

Gloom with no brightness in it. The repetition drives it home: darkness, gloom, no brightness. Yet there is good news here too. Christ entered the darkness of God’s judgment when he died in his people’s place (1 Thessalonians 5:9–10). That is why Paul can tell believers, “But you are not in darkness, brothers, for that day to surprise you like a thief” (1 Thessalonians 5:4). For those in Christ, the day of the Lord is the day of his appearing, a day of light.

The same mistake today. Many people still assume that God is on their side and that the last day will go well for them, without ever facing their own sin. It is the most dangerous comfort there is.

verseByVerse.quote: "I hate, I despise your feasts, and I take no delight in your solemn assemblies. Even though you offer me your burnt offerings and grain offerings, I will not accept them; and the peace offerings of your fattened animals, I will not look upon them. Take away from me the noise of your songs; to the melody of your harps I will not listen. But let justice roll down like waters, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God refuses worship from people who crush the poor; what he wants is justice and righteousness flowing through the whole of life like a river that never runs dry.

I hate, I despise your feasts. God’s strong words are aimed at Israel’s feasts, the festivals they celebrated so eagerly, and the word “your” is pointed. They were no longer God’s feasts; they had become Israel’s own.

I will not accept them. Every kind of offering is refused, and their skilful music is only noise. God is not against sacrifice or music; he commanded both. But worship offered by people who crush the poor on Monday is not worship to him. Samuel had said long before, “to obey is better than sacrifice” (1 Samuel 15:22).

Let justice roll down like waters. Many streambeds in Israel ran full in the rainy season and dry in summer. Israel’s justice was like that: it appeared for the festival and vanished in daily life. God wants justice that rolls down like a river in flood, and righteousness “like an ever-flowing stream” that never dries up, in the courts and in the marketplace.

What justice is. Most of us hear the word justice and think of courtrooms, or of a political slogan. The Hebrew word here, mishpat, is wider and more personal. Timothy Keller often pointed out that it means giving people what they are due, whether punishment or protection or care, and that the Bible ties it again and again to the widow, the orphan, the immigrant and the poor, the people with no one to speak for them. That is God’s own way: he “executes justice for the fatherless and the widow, and loves the sojourner” (Deuteronomy 10:18). Israel’s justice had dried up because their hearts leaned on money and comfort, and the poor were in the way.

Where the river starts. The gospel does not lower God’s standard. At the cross God showed “that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26): Christ received what we were due, so that we might receive what he was due. People who know they have been given what they never earned stop grudging others what they are owed. Justice that truly flows like a river can only come from hearts made new by that grace.

Worship beyond Sunday. Jesus pressed the same point on the religious leaders of his day. They tithed even their garden herbs, but neglected “the weightier matters of the law: justice and mercy and faithfulness” (Matthew 23:23). Christian worship is not only what happens on Sunday; Paul calls us to present our whole lives as “a living sacrifice” (Romans 12:1). This week that may mean paying a bill on time, paying a fair wage, or speaking up for the person nobody listens to.

Can we have justice without God? Many people today would turn Amos round: religion is the problem, they say, and we can pursue justice perfectly well without worship. Amos would indeed rather have honest courts than crowded festivals. But if the universe is only matter and chance, it is hard to say why the strong ought not to eat the weak; the conviction that the widow and the stranger matter came into the world through prophets like Amos, from a God who loves the sojourner. And justice with no one above us becomes a cause that must save us, with no mercy for those on the wrong side of it, or for ourselves when we fail it. Amos condemns religion without justice; he would condemn justice without God as firmly, because both leave us our own saviours. The gospel gives justice a source and a mercy. The Judge who demands it bore its sentence himself, “the righteous for the unrighteous” (1 Peter 3:18), and people forgiven like that can work hard for justice without hating anyone.

Does this make the gospel a political programme? No. Amos speaks to a people who claimed to worship the LORD, and demands that their worship show in courts, wages and markets. Christians must deal justly, help the poor and, as citizens, may rightly speak for the oppressed. But the gospel is the news of what Christ has done for sinners, not a party’s platform, and believers who agree on this verse may still differ in good conscience over the best laws and policies. The order matters: “Seek me and live” (5:4) comes first, and justice flows from those who have found him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Did you bring to me sacrifices and offerings during the forty years in the wilderness, O house of Israel? You shall take up Sikkuth your king, and Kiyyun your star-god—your images that you made for yourselves, and I will send you into exile beyond Damascus," says the LORD, whose name is the God of hosts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel’s worship had long been mixed with other gods, and the star-gods they made for themselves will go with them into exile far beyond Damascus.

Did you bring to me sacrifices and offerings? God looks back to the forty years in the wilderness. The question may expect the answer “Not mainly”: in those years the heart of Israel’s life with God was trust and obedience, not a busy system of sacrifices. Jeremiah makes a similar point: the command God gave was “Obey my voice, and I will be your God” (Jeremiah 7:23). Others read the question as pointing to Israel’s mixed worship even in the wilderness, when they offered sacrifices and still turned to idols. Both readings lead to the same place: God has always wanted hearts, not just rituals.

Sikkuth your king, and Kiyyun your star-god. Probably star-gods worshipped in Mesopotamia. Israel had begun to mix the worship of the LORD with the worship of the heavenly bodies. In the ESV’s reading, when they go into exile they will carry their idols with them, gods who cannot even carry themselves.

Into exile beyond Damascus. Further away than Israel’s familiar northern enemy, all the way to Assyria. It is a sobering end to a chapter that began with “Seek me and live”; yet that invitation still stands for all who come to God through Christ.

Stephen’s quotation. Stephen quoted these verses in the speech that ended in his stoning: “You took up the tent of Moloch and the star of your god Rephan” (Acts 7:43). His wording differs mainly because he was quoting the Greek translation of the Old Testament widely used in his day, and he says “beyond Babylon”, applying the words to Judah’s later exile as well. His point is Amos’s: God’s people had turned to false gods again and again and rejected his messengers, as his hearers were now rejecting Christ.

Uncertain wording. These verses are among the hardest in Amos. The names Sikkuth and Kiyyun are probably Mesopotamian star-gods (Kiyyun is likely Kaiwan, a name for the planet Saturn), but the Hebrew vowels seem to have been changed to echo a word for “detestable thing”, and the Greek translation read the first as “tent” (hence Stephen’s “tent of Moloch”). The verb in verse 26 can also be read as past (“you have carried”, as in the King James Version) rather than future (“you shall take up”), so that it describes idolatry Israel had already practised. The ESV’s future reading ties the idols to the coming exile.
verseByVerse.note: Rephan in Acts 7:43 is the Greek Old Testament's form of the star-god's name.

5.title: Let Justice Roll Down
5.overview:
Where we are. Chapters 3 to 6 are Amos’s sermons against Israel, and chapter 5 stands at their centre. After the summons “prepare to meet your God, O Israel!” (4:12), Amos sings a funeral song over a nation still eating, trading and worshipping around him.

The message. In God’s sight Israel is already dead, and yet the God who mourns it still calls, “Seek me and live” (v. 4). Seeking him does not mean visiting famous shrines or longing for a day of the LORD that will crown your success; it means turning to God himself, and that turning shows in courts where the poor get a fair hearing. God will not take songs from hands that crush the weak. He wants justice that never runs dry.

Why it was said. Israel’s prosperity rested on bribed judges and squeezed farmers, while the shrines at Bethel, Gilgal and Beersheba were crowded and the people looked forward to the day of the LORD as their day of triumph (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. Verses 1–17 are built like a ring around a centre. A funeral song (vv. 1–3) and a call to seek God and live (vv. 4–6) lead to justice turned to wormwood (v. 7); at the centre stands a hymn to the Creator who is also the Judge, “the LORD is his name” (vv. 8–9); then the ring closes in reverse, with injustice in the gate (vv. 10–13), a call to seek good and live (vv. 14–15), and wailing in every street (vv. 16–17). Then three blows to false security: the day of the LORD will be darkness (vv. 18–20); God hates feasts without justice (vv. 21–24); and worship mixed with star-gods will end in exile (vv. 25–27).

Where it leads. Chiefly by the need it exposes and by God’s character revealed in Christ. No people has ever produced justice like an ever-flowing stream; only Jesus lived a life in which worship and justice were never parted, and his righteousness is given to all who trust him. The darkness of the day of the LORD fell on him at noon on the cross (Matthew 27:45), so that for his people that day is light. And the call “Seek me and live” finds its answer in the one who “came to seek and to save the lost” (Luke 19:10): to find him is life.

For us. Ask what you seek when you go to church: God himself, or a place, a tradition, a feeling of safety. Then ask whether Sunday’s songs are matched by Monday’s dealings with workers, customers, tenants and the poor. Forgiven people do not earn God’s favour by justice; they let the river he has started in them run out into the world.
5.theology:
God's prophet mourns over a sinful nation before its fall, and God takes no pleasure in judgment (vv. 1-3, 16-17; Ezek 33:11).

Even in judgment God freely offers life to all who seek him, and seeking him means seeking God himself, not religious places or traditions (vv. 4-6, 14; Isa 55:6-7; John 14:6).

The Creator of the stars is the Judge of every courtroom and marketplace, and true repentance changes both what we love and how we act in public life (vv. 8-15; 4:13; Job 9:9; Mic 6:8).

The day of the LORD is darkness for all who presume on God's favour while living in sin; Christ entered that darkness so that believers are children of light (vv. 18-20; Matt 27:45; 1 Thess 5:4-5).

God rejects worship that is separated from justice and mercy, or mixed with other gods (vv. 21-27; Isa 1:11-17; 1 Sam 15:22; Matt 23:23; Rom 12:1; Acts 7:42-43).
5.examples:
The chapter is vivid: a bribe taken in the gate where the poor wait in vain, a stone house built with stolen grain and never lived in, and a man who escapes a lion and a bear only to be bitten by a snake at home.

Fine music sounds like noise in heaven, and over against a streambed that runs dry in summer stands God's river of justice that never stops flowing.

keyVerse.quote: But let justice roll down like waters, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream.
keyVerse.note: This is God’s answer to a nation busy with feasts and songs: not more religion but justice that never dries up. It stands beside the call “Seek me and live” (v. 4), because the river of justice can only flow from those who have found God himself. In Christ the righteousness God demands is first given, and then it begins to flow.

5.reflection:
God tells Israel to seek him and not Bethel, Gilgal or Beersheba (vv. 4–6). What “holy places” or religious habits are we tempted to seek instead of God himself, and how can we tell the difference?

Israel’s leaders hated “him who reproves in the gate” (v. 10). Why do people resent those who speak the truth about injustice? When have you found it costly to speak up, or easier to stay silent (v. 13)?

God says he hates Israel’s feasts and will not listen to their songs (vv. 21–23). What would it look like for our worship on Sunday to be matched by justice on Monday, in our work, our money and our neighbourhood?

Israel longed for the day of the LORD, sure it would be light for them (vv. 18–20). Why is it light for those in Christ, and how should that both humble and comfort us?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Woe to Those at Ease
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Comfort that makes us careless of God and blind to the ruin of others falls under his woe. Amos addresses the leaders of both kingdoms, at ease in Zion and secure on the hill of Samaria, who think themselves the elite of the first of nations (v. 1). Let them look at Calneh, Hamath and Gath, great cities already humbled, and ask why they should be spared, since they push away the thought of disaster while their own violence draws it near (vv. 2–3). He then shows their banquet: ivory couches, choice lamb and veal, idle songs, wine by the bowlful and the finest oils, but no grief over “the ruin of Joseph” (vv. 4–6). The first of the nations will be the first into exile (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: Comfort that makes us careless of God and blind to others' ruin is under God's woe.

verseByVerse.quote: "Woe to those who are at ease in Zion, and to those who feel secure on the mountain of Samaria, the notable men of the first of the nations, to whom the house of Israel comes! Pass over to Calneh, and see, and from there go to Hamath the great; then go down to Gath of the Philistines. Are you better than these kingdoms? Or is their territory greater than your territory, O you who put far away the day of disaster and bring near the seat of violence?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to the comfortable leaders of both kingdoms, who feel secure and forget that greater cities than theirs have already fallen.

Woe to those who are at ease in Zion. A woe was a cry of grief, the kind of word spoken at a funeral (compare 5:18). It falls on the leaders of both kingdoms, in Jerusalem and in Samaria. Their sin was complacency. Rich and powerful, they were sure that nothing could touch them: “the notable men of the first of the nations”, to whom ordinary people came for favours.

Pass over to Calneh, and see. Calneh and Hamath were important cities to the north, and Gath a Philistine city to the south-west. Gath had already been captured by Hazael of Syria (2 Kings 12:17), and Uzziah had broken down its wall (2 Chronicles 26:6). If proud cities like these could fall, why did Israel think it could not?

You who put far away the day of disaster. They pushed the day of disaster out of their minds while their injustice brought violence closer. “While people are saying, ‘There is peace and security,’ then sudden destruction will come upon them” (1 Thessalonians 5:3).

Complacency today. Complacency does not look like wickedness; it looks like success. Jesus told of a rich man who said to himself, “relax, eat, drink, be merry”, the very night his life was required of him (Luke 12:19–20). The church in Laodicea said, “I am rich, I have prospered, and I need nothing” (Revelation 3:17).

The idol of comfort. Few of us would say that comfort is our god. But an idol is easiest to spot by what we will not give up and what we most fear losing, and for many in prosperous countries that is comfort: the warm house, the smooth routine, the evening that asks nothing of us. It promises a life without pain and delivers a slow shrinking: a heart that must stay comfortable cannot afford to notice “the ruin of Joseph” (v. 6), because noticing would hurt; so it stops seeing, and calls the blindness peace. The leaders of Samaria were not monsters, only very well cushioned. The moralist answers with grim self-denial and the hedonist with more cushions, but both keep the self at the centre. The gospel does something stranger. It shows us a Lord who had every comfort of heaven and laid it aside, who had “nowhere to lay his head” (Luke 9:58), and who went to the cross for people at ease in Zion. When that love takes hold, comfort loses its grip: not because we despise good things, but because we have found a security that does not depend on them.

verseByVerse.quote: "Woe to those who lie on beds of ivory and stretch themselves out on their couches, and eat lambs from the flock and calves from the midst of the stall, who sing idle songs to the sound of the harp and like David invent for themselves instruments of music, who drink wine in bowls and anoint themselves with the finest oils, but are not grieved over the ruin of Joseph! Therefore they shall now be the first of those who go into exile, and the revelry of those who stretch themselves out shall pass away."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rich feast in luxury and feel nothing for their people’s ruin, so the “first” will be first into exile.

Woe to those who lie on beds of ivory. They recline on couches inlaid with carved ivory (compare 3:15), lazy and overfed. Most people in Israel ate meat only on special occasions; these ate choice lambs and stall-fattened calves as everyday food.

Like David. They think of themselves as great musicians like David. But David provided instruments to “offer praises to the LORD” (1 Chronicles 23:5); these people made music for themselves.

But are not grieved over the ruin of Joseph! Cups were not enough; they drank wine in bowls and used the most expensive oils. Then comes the heart of the charge. The northern tribes, the house of Joseph, were rotting from within, the poor were being crushed and judgment was coming, and they felt nothing.

The first of those who go into exile. A grim irony: they thought themselves “the first of the nations” (v. 1), so they will be the first into exile. “Pride goes before destruction” (Proverbs 16:18). The word for “revelry” (marzeah) names the feast of a closed drinking circle, and it will end.

Where the sin lies. God does not condemn feasting, music or perfume in themselves; Scripture is full of feasts and songs. The sin is enjoying good things while indifferent to the suffering around us and the spiritual ruin of God’s people. Nehemiah heard of Jerusalem’s ruin and “sat down and wept and mourned for days” (Nehemiah 1:4).

The one who grieved. When Jesus “drew near and saw the city, he wept over it” (Luke 19:41); and he did more than weep: he went to the cross to bear judgment for all who would turn to him. His love is what makes us able to love. His Spirit, who pours God’s love into our hearts (Romans 5:5), softens hard hearts so that they grieve over what grieves him. The test for us is simple: what breaks our hearts?

Uncertain wording. The verb translated “sing idle songs” occurs only here and probably means to improvise or strum carelessly; “invent for themselves instruments of music” may instead mean that they think themselves musicians like David. The picture is the same.
verseByVerse.note: Carved ivory inlays from furniture of this period have been found at Samaria.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–14 — I Abhor the Pride of Jacob
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God opposes the proud, and every victory we credit to our own strength will be taken away. The Lord swears by himself that he abhors the pride of Jacob and will hand over the city (v. 8). Amos pictures the siege that follows: ten men in one house all dead, a relative carrying out the bodies, and a survivor hushing any mention of the LORD’s name, as great houses and small are smashed (vv. 9–11). Israel has done something as senseless as racing horses on rocks, turning justice into poison, and then boasted of capturing “Horns” and rejoicing in “Nothing” (vv. 12–13). So God will raise up a nation to oppress it across the very borders it was proud of (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: God opposes the proud, and every victory we credit to our own strength will be taken away.

verseByVerse.quote: The Lord GOD has sworn by himself, declares the LORD, the God of hosts: "I abhor the pride of Jacob and hate his strongholds, and I will deliver up the city and all that is in it." And if ten men remain in one house, they shall die. And when one's relative, the one who anoints him for burial, shall take him up to bring the bones out of the house, and shall say to him who is in the innermost parts of the house, "Is there still anyone with you?" he shall say, "No"; and he shall say, "Silence! We must not mention the name of the LORD." For behold, the LORD commands, and the great house shall be struck down into fragments, and the little house into bits.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God swears by himself that he abhors Israel’s pride and will hand Samaria over to death, until survivors fear even to speak his name.

The Lord GOD has sworn by himself. God swears by himself, “since he had no one greater by whom to swear” (Hebrews 6:13), so the judgment is certain. “I abhor the pride of Jacob”: the things Israel was proudest of, its wealth, its fortresses and its success, God hates, because they had taken his place in their hearts. Yet this is the God who had brought Jacob up out of Egypt and made him his own (3:1–2); in their pride they had forgotten that everything they had came from his grace. Samaria will be handed over with everything in it. “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble” (1 Peter 5:5); and the God who swears by himself to judge pride once swore by himself to bless Abraham (Genesis 22:16), a promise kept in Christ.

Is there still anyone with you? Verses 9–10 picture the siege, when plague and death fill the city. Even if ten men shelter in one house, they will die. A relative comes to carry out the bodies and calls to someone hiding in the back room. “Is there still anyone with you?” The answer is “No”, followed by a chilling word: “Silence! We must not mention the name of the LORD.” The survivor fears that even speaking God’s name might draw more judgment. People who once used it lightly at their feasts are now terrified of it.

The LORD commands. No one is spared, neither the rich man’s great house nor the ordinary family’s little house, because the LORD commands it.

Uncertain wording. The words “the one who anoints him for burial” translate an unclear Hebrew word, often taken to mean “the one who burns him”. That may mean burning the bodies, which was not Israel’s custom but might be done in a plague, or burning spices in honour of the dead (2 Chronicles 16:14). Either way, the scene is of a city full of dead.

verseByVerse.quote: Do horses run on rocks? Does one plow there with oxen? But you have turned justice into poison and the fruit of righteousness into wormwood — you who rejoice in Lo-debar, who say, "Have we not by our own strength captured Karnaim for ourselves?" "For behold, I will raise up against you a nation, O house of Israel," declares the LORD, the God of hosts; "and they shall oppress you from Lebo-hamath to the Brook of the Arabah."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel’s injustice is as senseless as racing horses over rocks, and its boast of victories won by its own strength will end when God raises up a nation to crush it.

Do horses run on rocks? No one gallops horses over jagged rocks or ploughs rock with oxen; it would ruin the animals and achieve nothing. Yet Israel has done something just as absurd. It took justice, which should heal a society, and made it poison, and turned righteousness, which should bear sweet fruit, into wormwood, a bitter plant. Injustice is not only wicked. It is folly that goes against the grain of the world God made.

You who rejoice in Lo-debar. Lo-debar and Karnaim were towns east of the Jordan, probably won back in Jeroboam’s wars, and Israel celebrated these victories. But Amos plays on the names. As the ESV notes, Lo-debar means “nothing”, and Karnaim means “horns”, a symbol of strength. So they are celebrating a victory over Nothing, and boasting that by their own strength they took Horns.

By our own strength. Here is the deeper problem. God had warned Israel never to say, “My power and the might of my hand have gotten me this wealth”, “for it is he who gives you power to get wealth” (Deuteronomy 8:17–18). Paul asks, “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Corinthians 4:7). Every success is a gift of grace, and the only safe boast is in knowing the Lord (Jeremiah 9:24). Jesus, the true Israel, said the opposite: “the Son can do nothing of his own accord” (John 5:19).

I will raise up against you a nation. The nation is not named, but it was Assyria. The boundaries in verse 14 are chosen on purpose: they echo the very limits Jeroboam had won when “He restored the border of Israel from Lebo-hamath as far as the Sea of the Arabah” (2 Kings 14:25). All the territory Israel boasted of winning would be overrun. What we build in pride, God can take away; what we receive from his hand in humility, we hold as his gift.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 12 reads literally “Does one plow with oxen?”, which makes little sense, since everyone did. The ESV adds “there” (on the rocks); its footnote offers “Does one plow the sea with oxen?”, made by dividing the Hebrew letters differently. The point is the same.
verseByVerse.note: Lo-debar was the town where Jonathan's son Mephibosheth lived before David sent for him (2 Sam 9:4-5).

6.title: At Ease in Zion
6.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 6 closes Amos’s sermons (chapters 3–6), before the visions begin in chapter 7. Chapter 5 ended with exile “beyond Damascus” (5:27); now Amos turns from the courts and shrines to the dining rooms of the rich, in Samaria and in Jerusalem alike.

The message. Comfort that forgets God and feels nothing for the ruin of others is under God’s woe. The leaders of both kingdoms feel secure, feast on the best of everything and boast of victories won by their own strength, but they “are not grieved over the ruin of Joseph” (v. 6). God abhors that pride, and those who think themselves the first of the nations will be the first into exile.

Why it was said. Under Jeroboam II Israel had won back its old borders and grown rich (see the introduction). Recent victories at Lo-debar and Karnaim (v. 13) seemed to prove the nation strong and God pleased, while the poor were crushed beneath the banquets.

How the chapter makes its case. First a woe on the secure: let them look at great cities that have already fallen and ask whether they are any safer (vv. 1–3). Then the banquet itself, couches of ivory, choice meat, music, wine by the bowlful, and no grief for the nation’s ruin, so the revellers will lead the march into exile (vv. 4–7). God swears by himself that he abhors Jacob’s pride (v. 8), and pictures the siege: death in every house, and survivors afraid even to speak his name (vv. 9–11). Injustice is as absurd as racing horses over rocks, and Israel’s boast is in nothing (vv. 12–13), so God will raise up a nation to crush it from one border to the other (v. 14).

Where it leads. By contrast, and by God’s character revealed in Christ. Where Israel’s leaders lay on ivory and felt nothing, Jesus, “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9); he saw Jerusalem and wept over it, then went to the cross to bear the judgment it faced. Where Israel boasted, “by our own strength”, he “humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death” (Philippians 2:8). And the God who here swears by himself to judge also swore by himself to bless Abraham (Hebrews 6:13), a promise kept in Christ.

For us. Comfort is a quiet idol, and many of us live in more comfort than Samaria’s elite ever knew. Ask what breaks your heart, what you boast in, and whose ruin you have learned not to see. The answer is not grim self-denial but a Saviour whose love loosens comfort’s grip and teaches us to grieve, give and serve.
6.theology:
Complacency and a false sense of security are sins that God will judge (vv. 1-3; Luke 12:19-20; Rev 3:17; 1 Thess 5:3).

Enjoying God's good gifts while indifferent to the ruin of others and of God's people is under his woe (vv. 4-6; Neh 1:4; Rom 12:15; Luke 19:41).

God hates pride and opposes the proud (vv. 7-8; Prov 16:18; 1 Pet 5:5).

Injustice is not only wicked but foolish, contrary to the order of God's world (v. 12).

Every success is God's gift, and boasting in our own strength invites his judgment (vv. 13-14; Deut 8:17-18; 1 Cor 4:7; Jer 9:23-24).
6.examples:
Israel's leaders lounged on ivory couches and drank wine from bowls because cups were too small, with music and perfume and not one tear for the ruin outside. God does not forbid feasting; he grieves over hearts that feel nothing for others, and his Spirit can soften even ours.

Soon a survivor hushes anyone who mentions the name of God, and the nation that celebrated a victory over a town called Nothing discovers what its boasting was worth. Every success we have is a gift, to be held with open hands.

keyVerse.quote: Woe to those who are at ease in Zion, and to those who feel secure on the mountain of Samaria
keyVerse.note: The whole chapter grows from this first cry. The sin it names is not open violence but comfortable security: leaders so sure of their wealth and standing that they felt neither fear of God nor grief for others. It speaks with special force to prosperous believers, and it sends us to the Lord who left his own ease for our sake.

6.reflection:
Amos’s woe falls on those “at ease in Zion” who “feel secure” (v. 1). How can comfort and security become a danger to faith? Where do you see this in yourself or your church?

The rich were “not grieved over the ruin of Joseph” (v. 6). What sorrows around you, near or far, are you tempted not to see? What would it look like to grieve over them as Jesus wept over Jerusalem?

Israel boasted, “Have we not by our own strength captured Karnaim for ourselves?” (v. 13). In what successes do you most easily forget God’s hand, and how can you learn to receive them as gifts?

Jesus, though rich, became poor for our sake. How does his self-giving love free us from the grip of comfort without making us despise good gifts?
