"You say, 'Do not prophesy against Israel, and do not preach against the house of Isaac.'<sup>17</sup>Therefore thus says the LORD: "'Your wife shall be a prostitute in the city, and your sons and your daughters shall fall by the sword, and your land shall be divided up with a measuring line; you yourself shall die in an unclean land, and Israel shall surely go into exile away from its land.'"

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God hears those who stand in the gap, yet there comes a point when he measures his people and judgment must fall. In the first vision God is forming locusts to devour the regrowth that ordinary people lived on; Amos pleads “please forgive!” and the LORD relents (vv. 1–3). In the second a fire dries up the great deep and begins to eat the land; Amos cries “please cease!” and again the LORD relents (vv. 4–6). The third vision is quieter and final: the Lord stands with a plumb line beside a wall once built true, and Israel is found crooked. This time Amos does not pray. God will no longer pass by, and the shrines of Israel and the house of Jeroboam will fall (vv. 7–9).
verseByVerse.theology: God hears the prayers of those who stand in the gap, yet there comes a point when he measures his people by his standard and judgment must fall.

verseByVerse.quote: This is what the Lord GOD showed me: behold, he was forming locusts when the latter growth was just beginning to sprout, and behold, it was the latter growth after the king's mowings. When they had finished eating the grass of the land, I said, "O Lord GOD, please forgive! How can Jacob stand? He is so small!" The LORD relented concerning this: "It shall not be," said the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God shows Amos a plague of locusts about to strip the land; Amos pleads for forgiveness, and the LORD relents.

He was forming locusts. In the first of five visions God is forming locusts, like a potter shaping clay. The timing is terrible. The first cutting of grass, “the king’s mowings”, was probably the king’s share, taken as a tax. What grew back afterwards, “the latter growth”, was what ordinary people and their animals would live on. If locusts ate that, there would be nothing until the next year: famine.

O Lord GOD, please forgive! Amos takes no pleasure in announcing judgment. He prays at once for the very people who reject him. He does not argue that Israel deserves mercy. He appeals to their weakness: “How can Jacob stand? He is so small!” Israel thought itself strong and important (6:1, 13); Amos sees a small, helpless child before the power of God.

The LORD relented concerning this. God answered, and the plague did not come. Scripture tells several times of God relenting in response to prayer or repentance, as when Moses pleaded for Israel after the golden calf (Exodus 32:14).

That should make us pray. The warning, the prayer and the answer were all real: God meant to spare Israel for a time, through the prayer of his prophet. That should make us pray more, not less: “The prayer of a righteous person has great power” (James 5:16).

Where Christians differ. How can an unchanging God relent? Some Christians conclude that God truly changes his plans in response to what happens, and does not know or fix the future in advance. This commentary’s view: with the Reformed tradition and most of the church through history, God does not change his eternal purpose (Numbers 23:19; Malachi 3:6), but his purpose includes the means, and he has ordained that prayer is one of the means by which he carries it out. “Relent” describes truly what God does in history, in answer to real prayer, without implying that he was taken by surprise.

verseByVerse.quote: This is what the Lord GOD showed me: behold, the Lord GOD was calling for a judgment by fire, and it devoured the great deep and was eating up the land. Then I said, "O Lord GOD, please cease! How can Jacob stand? He is so small!" The LORD relented concerning this: "This also shall not be," said the Lord GOD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Amos sees a fire that dries up even the great deep; he begs God to stop, and again the LORD relents.

A judgment by fire. In the second vision the fire is so hot that it dries up “the great deep”, the vast waters under the earth that fed springs and rivers, and then starts eating up the land. It may picture a burning drought so severe that nothing survives.

O Lord GOD, please cease! This time Amos does not even say “forgive”. He simply begs God to stop, and again God relents. Twice judgment is held back because one man stood between God and the people. God once looked for someone to “stand in the breach before me for the land” and found none (Ezekiel 22:30). Here he found one.

Christ the Intercessor. Amos points us to a greater Intercessor. Jesus Christ “always lives to make intercession” for those who come to God through him (Hebrews 7:25). Amos could only delay judgment; Christ took it on himself, so that his people are spared for ever. Because he pleads for us, and his Spirit helps us in our weakness when we pray (Romans 8:26), every Christian can pray for family, church and nation with the compassion Amos showed.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew behind “calling for a judgment by fire” is unusual, literally “calling to contend by fire”; some scholars divide the letters differently to read “calling for a shower of fire”. Either way, God summons fire as his instrument of judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: This is what he showed me: behold, the Lord was standing beside a wall built with a plumb line, with a plumb line in his hand. And the LORD said to me, "Amos, what do you see?" And I said, "A plumb line." Then the Lord said, "Behold, I am setting a plumb line in the midst of my people Israel; I will never again pass by them; the high places of Isaac shall be made desolate, and the sanctuaries of Israel shall be laid waste, and I will rise against the house of Jeroboam with the sword."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God measures Israel with his plumb line, finds it crooked, and will no longer pass over its sin: its shrines and its royal house will fall.

A wall built with a plumb line. The third vision is quieter and final. A plumb line is a weight on a string that builders used to check whether a wall was upright, because the string always hangs straight. The Lord stands beside a wall that was built true in the beginning. Israel had been built straight by God, and now he comes to test whether it still is.

I am setting a plumb line in the midst of my people. God will measure them by his own standard, not by their opinion of themselves or by comparison with the nations around them. And the wall is badly crooked. Isaiah uses the same picture: “And I will make justice the line, and righteousness the plumb line” (Isaiah 28:17).

I will never again pass by them. God will no longer overlook their sins. This time Amos does not pray. The measurement has been taken, and there is nothing to say. There comes a point when a people’s sin is so settled that God’s patience ends.

The high places of Isaac. Judgment will fall on Israel’s religion and its royal family. The high places (hilltop shrines) and sanctuaries where Israel worshipped would be ruined. Isaac stands here for the nation descended from him. And God will rise “against the house of Jeroboam with the sword”: Jeroboam’s son Zechariah reigned only six months before he was assassinated (2 Kings 15:8–10).

What is God’s plumb line for us? His law, and above all Jesus Christ himself, the only perfectly upright life ever lived. Measured against him, every one of us is crooked. That is why we need not only a plumb line but a Saviour. The One who measures us is the One who died for crooked people and makes them new.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “plumb line” (anak) appears nowhere else in the Old Testament (see the note). Some think it means “tin”, picturing a wall of tin; but a measuring line fits verse 8 well, and most translations keep it.
verseByVerse.note: The Hebrew word (anak) occurs only in these verses. Some scholars think it means "tin" rather than a plumb line, but the ESV's rendering remains the usual one.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: No human authority can silence the word of God, and those who try bring its judgment on themselves. Amaziah, priest of the royal shrine at Bethel, reports Amos to King Jeroboam as a conspirator, twisting his words into a threat against the king (vv. 10–11). Then he tells Amos to go back to Judah, earn his living there and never prophesy again at the king’s sanctuary (vv. 12–13). Amos answers that he is no professional prophet but a herdsman and fig-tender whom the LORD himself took from the flock and sent to his people (vv. 14–15). Because Amaziah tried to silence God, God’s word now falls on him and on his house, and Israel will still go into exile (vv. 16–17).
verseByVerse.theology: No human authority can silence the word of God, and those who oppose it bring judgment on themselves.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Amaziah the priest of Bethel sent to Jeroboam king of Israel, saying, "Amos has conspired against you in the midst of the house of Israel. The land is not able to bear all his words. For thus Amos has said, "'Jeroboam shall die by the sword, and Israel must go into exile away from his land.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The priest of the royal shrine reports Amos to the king as a traitor, twisting God’s message into a political plot.

Amos has conspired against you. Amaziah was the chief priest at Bethel, the royal shrine. Amos was not plotting a rebellion; he was preaching God’s word. But to a religious leader who served the government, a prophet who criticised the king looked like a political threat.

The land is not able to bear all his words. Amaziah is right in a way he did not intend: God’s word was too heavy for a nation built on injustice.

Jeroboam shall die by the sword. Amaziah’s report twists Amos’s words. Amos had said God would rise against “the house of Jeroboam” (v. 9), meaning his dynasty; Amaziah makes it a personal threat against the king. In fact Jeroboam himself died in peace (2 Kings 14:29), and it was his son who was killed. Amaziah also leaves things out: the visions, the call to repentance and Amos’s prayers for the people. Opponents of God’s word often quote it selectively to make it sound as bad as possible.

The same charge against Jesus. The same fear moved the religious leaders against Jesus: “If we let him go on like this … the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation” (John 11:48). And the same twisted report was carried to the governor: “We found this man misleading our nation and forbidding us to give tribute to Caesar, and saying that he himself is Christ, a king” (Luke 23:2).

verseByVerse.quote: And Amaziah said to Amos, "O seer, go, flee away to the land of Judah, and eat bread there, and prophesy there, but never again prophesy at Bethel, for it is the king's sanctuary, and it is a temple of the kingdom."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Amaziah orders Amos to go home to Judah and earn his living there, because Bethel belongs to the king.

O seer, go, flee away. We are not told how the king replied, but Amaziah confronts Amos directly. Calling him “seer” (an old word for a prophet) may be a sneer. “Go, flee away to the land of Judah”: go back where you came from. “Eat bread there”: earn your living there. Amaziah assumes that Amos is a religious professional preaching for money, as Amaziah himself served the king for his living. He cannot imagine a man who speaks simply because God has sent him.

It is the king’s sanctuary. Bethel was “the king’s sanctuary” and “a temple of the kingdom”. Amaziah does not call it God’s house. Religion had become a department of the state, there to support the king’s power and bless the nation’s success (1 Kings 12:31–33). In such a place a prophet who speaks against the king is not welcome.

The same trap today. Churches fall into the same trap whenever they exist to bless those in political power, of any party, or want preaching that is comfortable and never challenges. Paul warned of people who “will accumulate for themselves teachers to suit their own passions” (2 Timothy 4:3). The church belongs to Christ, not to any king or nation.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Amos answered and said to Amaziah, "I was no prophet, nor a prophet's son, but I was a herdsman and a dresser of sycamore figs. But the LORD took me from following the flock, and the LORD said to me, 'Go, prophesy to my people Israel.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Amos is no professional prophet but a farmer whom the LORD himself took from the flock and sent to his people.

I was no prophet, nor a prophet’s son. Amos is not intimidated. He is not denying that God has made him speak for him. He means he was not a professional prophet and did not belong to a band of trained prophets, such as “the sons of the prophets” found at Bethel in Elisha’s day (2 Kings 2:3). He did not choose this work to make a living. He was a herdsman and “a dresser of sycamore figs”, which probably meant nicking the fruit of a kind of fig tree so that it would ripen. It was ordinary farm work, not religious training.

The LORD took me from following the flock. Here is Amos’s authority: he did not seek the role; God interrupted his life. God said almost the same to David: “I took you from the pasture, from following the sheep” (2 Samuel 7:8). And God called Israel “my people”. Amaziah called Bethel the king’s temple, but Israel belonged to God, and God had the right to speak to them.

No credentials but his sending. Jesus faced the same sneer: “How is it that this man has learning, when he has never studied?” His answer was Amos’s: “My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me” (John 7:15–16).

Ordinary people called. God still delights to use ordinary people: “not many of you were wise according to worldly standards, not many were powerful”, “But God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise” (1 Corinthians 1:26–27). What matters is not our credentials but God’s call. And when human authorities order God’s servants to be quiet, the apostles’ answer still stands: “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29).

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew has no verb, so the words can be read “I was no prophet” (until God called him) or “I am no prophet” (of the professional kind); the ESV notes both. Either way his authority is God’s call alone.
verseByVerse.note: Sycamore figs were a cheap fruit that had to be nicked to ripen.

verseByVerse.quote: Now therefore hear the word of the LORD. "You say, 'Do not prophesy against Israel, and do not preach against the house of Isaac.' Therefore thus says the LORD: "'Your wife shall be a prostitute in the city, and your sons and your daughters shall fall by the sword, and your land shall be divided up with a measuring line; you yourself shall die in an unclean land, and Israel shall surely go into exile away from its land.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because Amaziah tried to silence God’s word, that word now falls on him and his house, and Israel will still go into exile.

Now therefore hear the word of the LORD. Amaziah had told Amos to stop speaking; Amos answers by speaking again, quoting the priest’s own order back to him. The word for “preach” is literally “drip”, perhaps a sneer at prophets’ words as drivel (compare Micah 2:6). The man who thought he could silence God now hears God’s word fall on himself.

Your wife shall be a prostitute in the city. The words describe what happens when a city is conquered. Amaziah’s wife would be left destitute, forced into prostitution to survive or abused by the invaders. His children would be killed, and his land measured out and given to foreigners. And he himself, a priest whose life revolved around ritual purity, would die “in an unclean land”, a pagan country far from home. The exile Amaziah had tried to stop Amos announcing came anyway: “So Israel was exiled from their own land to Assyria” (2 Kings 17:23).

His family’s suffering. It is hard to read that his wife and children suffer for his sin. Amos is describing what conquest would do to a priest’s household; Scripture insists that before God each person answers for his own sin (Ezekiel 18:20), and the innocent who suffer in war are not forgotten by him.

Not revenge but judgment. This is not Amos taking personal revenge. It is God’s judgment on a religious leader who used his office to shut God’s mouth. But the warning is for everyone. Each of us can respond to God’s word like Amaziah, telling it to go away, or like Amos, who heard it, prayed and obeyed, not by his own courage but because the LORD took him and sent him. “If I were still trying to please man, I would not be a servant of Christ” (Galatians 1:10).

7.title: The Plumb Line
7.overview:
Where we are. The sermons of chapters 3 to 6 are over, and the last part of the book (chapters 7–9) is built around five visions. Chapter 7 holds the first three, and then breaks off for the only story in Amos: his clash with the priest of Bethel.

The message. God hears the prayer of a man who stands between him and a guilty people, and twice he holds back judgment. But when he measures his people by his own plumb line and they will not hear his word, judgment must come. A nation can try to silence God’s word; it cannot stop it, and the attempt seals its own fate.

Why it was said. Bethel was the royal shrine of the northern kingdom, and its religion served the king and blessed the nation’s success (see the introduction). A herdsman from Judah announcing the fall of Jeroboam’s house was, to its priest, simply a traitor.

How the chapter makes its case. In the first vision God forms locusts to strip the land; Amos cries “please forgive!” and the LORD relents (vv. 1–3). In the second a fire consumes the great deep; Amos begs “please cease!” and again the LORD relents (vv. 4–6). In the third the Lord stands with a plumb line, finds Israel crooked, and this time there is no prayer: the shrines and the royal house will fall (vv. 7–9). The story that follows shows why. Amaziah reports Amos to the king as a conspirator (vv. 10–11) and orders him home to Judah (vv. 12–13). Amos answers that the LORD took him from the flock and sent him (vv. 14–15), and the word Amaziah tried to silence falls on Amaziah himself (vv. 16–17).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by the need it exposes. Amos the intercessor, praying for people who despised him, points to Christ, who “always lives to make intercession” for his people (Hebrews 7:25) and who did not merely delay judgment but bore it. The plumb line exposes every one of us as crooked, and only one life has ever measured true. And the rejected prophet is a pattern of the Son, sent by the Father, reported to the authorities as a threat to the nation and driven out by the religious leaders of his day.

For us. Pray for your church, your family and your nation as Amos did, appealing not to their merit but to God’s mercy. Let God’s word measure you instead of measuring yourself against others. And when that word is unwelcome, to you or to those in power, remember that Christ’s church belongs to him, not to any king.
7.theology:
God reveals his coming judgments so that his servants may pray and his people may repent (vv. 1, 4, 7; 3:7).

God hears the intercession of his people and has ordained prayer as a means of carrying out his unchanging purposes (vv. 2-3, 5-6; Exod 32:14; Num 23:19; Jas 5:16).

Christ is the perfect Intercessor, who not only pleads for his people but bears their judgment (vv. 2, 5; Heb 7:25; Rom 8:34).

God measures his people by his own standard, and his patience has a limit (vv. 7-9; Isa 28:17).

Religion that serves political power rather than God will oppose God's word (vv. 10-13; John 11:48; 2 Tim 4:3-4).

God's call, not human credentials, gives authority to speak his word, and his servants must obey God rather than men (vv. 14-15; 2 Sam 7:8; 1 Cor 1:26-27; Acts 4:19-20; 5:29).

Those who try to silence God's word bring judgment on themselves, and his word will be fulfilled (vv. 16-17; 2 Kgs 15:8-10; 17:23).
7.examples:
Amos sees locusts devouring the only grass left after the king has taken his share, and a fire so hot it dries up the waters under the earth, and both times he begs mercy for the people who despise him. Intercession like that is still the calling of every Christian, and Christ is the Intercessor behind all our prayers.

Then a builder's string hangs straight beside a leaning wall, and a priest reports a preacher to the king as a traitor in a temple he calls the king's sanctuary instead of God's house. A countryman answers that God took him from the flock. What gives a person the right to speak for God is God's call, not a title or a salary.

keyVerse.quote: Behold, I am setting a plumb line in the midst of my people Israel; I will never again pass by them
keyVerse.note: The plumb line is the turning point of the chapter. Twice Amos’s prayer held back judgment, but when God measures his people by his own straight line, the crookedness is plain and he will no longer pass by. Every reader is measured by the same line, and only Christ has ever stood true; in him the crooked find mercy.

7.reflection:
Amos prayed for the very people who rejected him, appealing not to their goodness but to their weakness: “He is so small!” (vv. 2, 5). What can we learn from his prayers about how to pray for our church, our family or our nation?

God’s plumb line measures his people by his standard, not by their opinion of themselves (vv. 7–8). How do we tend to measure ourselves instead? What does it mean that Christ is both the plumb line and the Saviour of the crooked?

Amaziah called Bethel “the king’s sanctuary” and wanted a prophet who would not trouble the powerful (vv. 12–13). In what ways can churches today become chaplains to power or comfort? How can we guard against it?

Amos had no credentials except that “the LORD took me” (v. 15). How does God’s call give courage to ordinary believers to speak and live faithfully when it is unwelcome?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — A Basket of Summer Fruit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel is ripe for judgment, and the end has come. In the fourth vision God shows Amos a basket of summer fruit, the last harvest of the year, ripe and soon to spoil, and the Hebrew word for it sounds like the word for “end” (vv. 1–2a). As with the plumb line, God declares that he will never again pass by his people (v. 2b). The joyful songs of the temple will turn into wailing, and Amos hears the broken cries of that day: bodies everywhere, cast out, and then only silence (v. 3). The vision is short, and its brevity is part of the message: the time for warnings is ending.
verseByVerse.theology: Israel is ripe for judgment, and the end is at hand.

verseByVerse.quote: This is what the Lord GOD showed me: behold, a basket of summer fruit. And he said, "Amos, what do you see?" And I said, "A basket of summer fruit." Then the LORD said to me, "The end has come upon my people Israel; I will never again pass by them. The songs of the temple shall become wailings in that day," declares the Lord GOD. "So many dead bodies!" "They are thrown everywhere!" "Silence!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
A basket of ripe summer fruit tells Amos that Israel is ripe for the end, and its songs will become wailing over the dead.

A basket of summer fruit. The fourth vision looks harmless: ripe figs and other fruit picked at the end of the harvest season. The meaning lies in the sound of the words. The Hebrew for “summer fruit” (qayits) and for “end” (qets) sound alike. Like fruit at the end of summer, Israel is ripe, ready for harvest and soon to rot.

I will never again pass by them. As in the plumb line vision (7:8), Amos asks for no mercy. The time for warnings is ending.

The songs of the temple shall become wailings. The joyful songs of worship will turn into wailing. The last words come in short, broken cries, like a survivor walking through a ruined city with too many dead to bury, falling silent in horror (compare 6:10).

Ripe, but not yet picked. Israel’s end came because God’s long patience had been refused. The same patience is held out now, “not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance” (2 Peter 3:9); the time to turn to Christ is before the harvest.

Uncertain wording. “Temple” may also be “palace” (the ESV notes this), perhaps meaning the palace singing women. The cries ending verse 3 are compressed in Hebrew and their division uncertain; the ESV sets them out as three broken cries.
verseByVerse.note: The Gezer Calendar, a Hebrew inscription from about the tenth century BC, ends the farming year with a month of summer fruit.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God remembers every act of dishonesty against the poor, and he will turn the joy of the oppressor into grief. Amos lets us overhear Israel’s merchants: they keep the new moon and the Sabbath, but cannot wait for them to end so that they can cheat with small measures and heavy weights, sell the sweepings with the grain, and buy the poor into slavery for silver or a pair of sandals (vv. 4–6). God swears that he will never forget any of it, and the land will tremble and heave like the Nile (vv. 7–8). On that day the sun will go down at noon, feasts will become funerals, and the grief will be like mourning for an only son (vv. 9–10).
verseByVerse.theology: God remembers every act of dishonesty against the poor, and he will turn the joy of the oppressor into grief.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear this, you who trample on the needy and bring the poor of the land to an end, saying, "When will the new moon be over, that we may sell grain? And the Sabbath, that we may offer wheat for sale, that we may make the ephah small and the shekel great and deal deceitfully with false balances, that we may buy the poor for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals and sell the chaff of the wheat?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel is ripe for judgment because its merchants keep the holy days but long to get back to cheating the poor and buying the needy as slaves.

You who trample on the needy. Amos returns to the sin he has exposed from the beginning (2:6–8). The powerful trample the needy, and aim to “bring the poor of the land to an end”, pushing them off their land and out of existence.

When will the new moon be over? Amos lets us overhear the merchants. They kept the religious holidays, closing their shops on the new moon festival at the start of each month (Numbers 10:10) and on the Sabbath. But their hearts were in the marketplace. They sat through worship thinking, “When will this be over, so I can get back to making money?”

Make the ephah small and the shekel great. An ephah was a measure for grain (about 22 litres, as the ESV notes), and a shekel was a weight used to weigh silver (about 11 grams). A small ephah gave the buyer less grain and a heavy shekel made him pay more silver: the scales were tipped both ways. God’s law demanded “just balances, just weights, a just ephah” (Leviticus 19:36), and “A false balance is an abomination to the LORD” (Proverbs 11:1).

Buy the poor for silver. The poor, cheated until they fell into debt, were then bought as slaves for silver or for the price of a pair of sandals (2:6). Meanwhile the merchants sold the sweepings of the threshing floor mixed in with the grain, profiting even from rubbish.

A divided heart. Here is a heart religious on the holy day and ruthless on the business day. Jesus said, “You cannot serve God and money” (Luke 16:13). How we treat customers, employees and those who owe us money is as much a matter of worship as how we sing on Sunday. The law of just weights came from the God who had set Israel free from slavery; Leviticus 19:36 goes on, “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt”. Our reason for honest dealing is Christ, who “became poor” for our sakes (2 Corinthians 8:9), and his Spirit loosens greed’s grip on the heart.

Is trading on Sunday wrong? The sin here is greedy hearts that resented the day of rest and cheated the poor. The Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ (Colossians 2:16–17), and no day binds the conscience; but a heart that cannot stop for God shows what it worships. Christians gladly set apart the Lord’s Day for worship and rest as a gift. Many godly brothers, with the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, hold it as the Christian Sabbath, and this commentary honours them.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD has sworn by the pride of Jacob: "Surely I will never forget any of their deeds. Shall not the land tremble on this account, and everyone mourn who dwells in it, and all of it rise like the Nile, and be tossed about and sink again, like the Nile of Egypt?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God swears never to forget what the merchants have done, and the land itself will heave like the Nile.

The LORD has sworn by the pride of Jacob. The oath is solemn. The merchants thought no one noticed their small cheats; God keeps every record.

Surely I will never forget any of their deeds. A terrifying thought for anyone outside Christ, and a great comfort for the poor who have been cheated: no wrong done to them is lost. And for those who trust in Christ, God makes an astonishing promise: “I will remember their sins no more”, because Christ has borne them (Hebrews 8:12).

Shall not the land tremble? Such sin makes even the land tremble. It will rise and sink like the Nile, which rose every year in flood and fell again. This may picture a great earthquake, like the one mentioned at the start of the book (1:1).

Uncertain wording. “The pride of Jacob” can be read two ways. It may be irony, God swearing by Israel’s settled arrogance (compare 6:8), or a title for God himself, Jacob’s true pride, much as Samuel calls God “the Glory of Israel” (1 Samuel 15:29). Either way the oath is certain.

verseByVerse.quote: "And on that day," declares the Lord GOD, "I will make the sun go down at noon and darken the earth in broad daylight. I will turn your feasts into mourning and all your songs into lamentation; I will bring sackcloth on every waist and baldness on every head; I will make it like the mourning for an only son and the end of it like a bitter day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the day of the LORD God will darken the sun at noon and turn Israel’s feasts into funerals, with grief like mourning for an only son.

I will make the sun go down at noon. On that day, the day of the LORD, the sun will set at noon. Darkness at midday means everything is turned upside down; the day of the LORD is “darkness, and not light” (5:18). A great eclipse of the sun in 763 BC, total in Assyria and noted in its records, fell within Amos’s lifetime and may have given the picture extra force.

The mourning for an only son. The merchants’ feasts will become funerals, with sackcloth and shaved heads, the signs of mourning. The deepest grief of all is mourning for an only son, when parents lose their only child and with him their future.

Darkness at the cross. These words find a deeper echo in the Gospels. When the only Son of God hung on the cross, “there was darkness over the whole land” from about noon “until the ninth hour, while the sun’s light failed” (Luke 23:44–45). Zechariah foretold that people would look on the one they pierced and “mourn for him, as one mourns for an only child” (Zechariah 12:10). God gave “his only Son” (John 3:16) and “did not spare” him (Romans 8:32). The darkness of judgment fell on him so that it need not fall on us.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–14 — Not a Famine of Bread
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A fearful judgment is for God to fall silent to those who would not listen. Israel had silenced its prophets and sent Amos away; now God warns of a famine worse than any lack of bread, a famine of hearing his words. People will stagger from sea to sea and run to and fro looking for a word from the LORD and will not find it (vv. 11–12). Even the strongest and most beautiful of the young will faint with thirst, and those who swore by the idols of Samaria, Dan and Beersheba will fall and never rise again (vv. 13–14). What they trusted in place of God’s word will fail them.
verseByVerse.theology: A fearful judgment is for God to fall silent to those who would not listen.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, the days are coming," declares the Lord GOD, "when I will send a famine on the land— not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the LORD. They shall wander from sea to sea, and from north to east; they shall run to and fro, to seek the word of the LORD, but they shall not find it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because Israel silenced God’s prophets, God will one day fall silent, and people will search everywhere for a word from him and not find it.

Not a famine of bread. Israel had known famine and drought (4:6–8). Now God warns of something worse: a famine “of hearing the words of the LORD”. Israel had told the prophets to be quiet (2:12), and Amaziah had ordered Amos away from Bethel (7:12–13). God will give them what they asked for: he will stop speaking. There had been such a time before, when “the word of the LORD was rare in those days” (1 Samuel 3:1).

They shall not find it. When disaster comes, people will wander everywhere searching for a word from God. God had warned in Proverbs, “they will seek me diligently but will not find me” (Proverbs 1:28). They wanted his word only when it was too late.

For a world full of Bibles. It is possible to have God’s word close at hand and never truly hear it, until the heart grows so hard that it cannot hear at all. “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts” (Hebrews 3:15). Jesus said, “Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God” (Matthew 4:4). And Jesus himself is God’s final Word. When many turned away, Peter said, “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life” (John 6:68).

Why is God so silent? A common complaint today is that if God were real he would make himself plain. Amos turns it on its head. Israel did not suffer from too little revelation but from a great deal that it would not hear. It silenced the prophets (2:12) and sent Amos home (7:12), and at last God gave it what it asked for. The silence we resent may be less a proof of God’s absence than the echo of our own preference; most of us want a God who speaks when we need him and stays quiet when he would correct us. Yet the deepest answer to God’s silence is not an argument but an event. On the cross the Son cried, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46), and heaven gave no answer. He went into the famine of the word so that no one who comes to him will ever finally meet it. God has not stopped speaking; he “has spoken to us by his Son” (Hebrews 1:2), and the question is whether we will listen.

verseByVerse.quote: "In that day the lovely virgins and the young men shall faint for thirst. Those who swear by the Guilt of Samaria, and say, 'As your god lives, O Dan,' and, 'As the Way of Beersheba lives,' they shall fall, and never rise again."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even the strongest young people will faint with thirst, and all who swore by Samaria’s idols will fall, never to rise again.

The lovely virgins and the young men shall faint for thirst. Even the strongest and most beautiful of the nation will faint, a thirst that also pictures the spiritual famine of verse 11. A generation cut off from God’s word withers.

Those who swear by the Guilt of Samaria. They have drunk from false wells. They swear oaths by false gods: “the Guilt of Samaria”, some idol worshipped in the capital; the god of Dan, where Jeroboam son of Nebat had set up a golden calf (1 Kings 12:28–30; 2 Kings 10:29); and “the Way of Beersheba”, the pilgrimage road to the southern shrine (5:5). To swear by something is to trust it. They trusted their idols and their pilgrimages, and “they shall fall, and never rise again”, echoing Amos’s funeral song for Israel (5:2).

Living water. Only the living God can satisfy that thirst. Jesus stood up at a feast in Jerusalem and cried, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37). The famine Amos foretold is not God’s last word to those who come to his Son.

Uncertain wording. “The Guilt of Samaria” may be a scornful play on the name of a goddess, Ashima, later worshipped in the region (2 Kings 17:30), or a mocking name for the calf idol. “The Way of Beersheba” is unusual; it may mean the pilgrim road or, with a slight change, the god of Beersheba.

8.title: A Famine of the Word
8.overview:
Where we are. After the clash with Amaziah at Bethel (7:10–17), the visions resume. The fourth vision, a basket of summer fruit, repeats the plumb line’s verdict that God will “never again pass by” Israel (7:8); chapter 9 brings the fifth.

The message. Israel is ripe for the end, and the reason is the one Amos has pressed from the start: people who keep the holy days but cannot wait to get back to cheating and enslaving the poor. God never forgets such deeds. He will turn their feasts into funerals, and, worst of all, the people who silenced his prophets will one day search for his word and not find it.

Why it was said. Israel’s merchants observed the new moon and the Sabbath while rigging their measures and buying the poor into slavery, and its priest had just ordered God’s prophet out of Bethel (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. The vision comes first: ripe summer fruit, and in Hebrew the word sounds like “end”, so the temple songs will become wailing over the dead (vv. 1–3). Then the charge: merchants who resent the holy days, make the ephah small and the shekel great, and buy “the needy for a pair of sandals” (vv. 4–6). God swears never to forget, and the land will heave like the Nile (vv. 7–8). On that day the sun will set at noon and every feast will become mourning “like the mourning for an only son” (vv. 9–10). Last comes the worst judgment of all: not a famine of bread but of hearing the words of the LORD, while the young faint with thirst and the worshippers of Samaria’s idols fall for good (vv. 11–14).

Where it leads. By pattern and by the need it exposes. Amos’s picture of noon darkness and mourning for an only son found a deeper echo when “there was darkness over the whole land” as God’s only Son hung on the cross (Luke 23:44), bearing the judgment his people deserved. There the Son cried to his Father and heaven was silent; he entered the famine of the word so that all who come to him may hear God speak. The God who “will never forget” their deeds says of those in Christ, “I will remember their sins no more” (Hebrews 8:12).

For us. Our work and our trading are as much a matter of worship as our singing: honest measures, fair prices and fair wages honour the God who set his people free. And God’s word, open on the table in many homes, is a gift that can be refused until it is gone. Listen today, and come to Christ, the living Word.
8.theology:
There comes a time when a people is ripe for judgment and God's patience ends (vv. 1-3; 7:8).

Religious observance combined with dishonesty in business is hateful to God; he demands just weights and fair dealing (vv. 4-6; Lev 19:35-36; Prov 11:1; Luke 16:13).

God never forgets the deeds of the unrepentant, yet in Christ he remembers his people's sins no more (v. 7; Heb 8:12).

The day of the LORD turns celebration into mourning; its darkness fell on Christ, God's only Son, at the cross (vv. 9-10; Luke 23:44-45; Zech 12:10; John 3:16).

God's word is life, and to lose it is a worse famine than lack of bread; those who reject it may find it withdrawn (vv. 11-12; 1 Sam 3:1; Prov 1:28; Matt 4:4; Heb 3:15).

Trusting in idols and religious pilgrimages leads to a fall with no recovery; only Christ has the words of eternal life (vv. 13-14; John 6:68).
8.examples:
A merchant counts the hours until the Sabbath is over, with a scale weighted one way for grain and the other way for silver, and sells the chaff swept up from the floor as wheat. How we treat customers, employees and debtors is as much worship as anything we sing on Sunday.

The sun goes down at noon on a feast day, and people run from sea to sea looking for a word from God that they once told to be quiet. Today, while we can hear his voice, is the time to listen.

keyVerse.quote: not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the LORD.
keyVerse.note: This is the climax of the chapter and its most searching threat. A people who silenced God’s prophets would one day find that God had fallen silent. It warns every generation with Bibles in reach not to treat God’s word lightly, and it sends us to Christ, the living Word, who has “the words of eternal life” (John 6:68).

8.reflection:
The merchants kept the holy days but could not wait to get back to business (v. 5). Where do you see a divided heart, religious on Sunday and different on Monday, in our culture or in yourself? What would honest dealing look like in your work this week?

God says, “Surely I will never forget any of their deeds” (v. 7), yet to those in Christ he promises to remember their sins no more. How does this warning comfort those who have been wronged, and how does the promise comfort those who have done wrong?

Amos speaks of darkness at noon and mourning “for an only son” (vv. 9–10). How do these words help us understand what happened at the cross?

God warns of a famine “of hearing the words of the LORD” (v. 11). How can people surrounded by Bibles still suffer that famine? What helps you to hear God’s word and not harden your heart?

"Did I not bring up Israel from the land of Egypt, and the Philistines from Caphtor and the Syrians from Kir?<sup>8</sup>Behold, the eyes of the Lord GOD are upon the sinful kingdom, and I will destroy it from the surface of the ground, except that I will not utterly destroy the house of Jacob," declares the LORD.<sup>9</sup>"For behold, I will command, and shake the house of Israel among all the nations as one shakes with a sieve, but no pebble shall fall to the earth.<sup>10</sup>All the sinners of my people shall die by the sword, who say, 'Disaster shall not overtake or meet us.'<sup>11</sup>"In that day I will raise up the booth of David that is fallen and repair its breaches, and raise up its ruins and rebuild it as in the days of old,<sup>12</sup>that they may possess the remnant of Edom and all the nations who are called by my name," declares the LORD who does this.<sup>13</sup>"Behold, the days are coming," declares the LORD, "when the plowman shall overtake the reaper and the treader of grapes him who sows the seed; the mountains shall drip sweet wine, and all the hills shall flow with it.<sup>14</sup>I will restore the fortunes of my people Israel, and they shall rebuild the ruined cities and inhabit them; they shall plant vineyards and drink their wine, and they shall make gardens and eat their fruit.<sup>15</sup>I will plant them on their land, and they shall never again be uprooted out of the land that I have given them," says the LORD your God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — No Escape and a Sifting
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Nowhere is beyond God’s reach and no privilege exempts his people from judgment, yet in judgment he keeps a remnant. Amos sees the Lord at the altar commanding the shrine to fall on the worshippers (v. 1). Grave, sky, mountain, sea and exile all fail as hiding places (vv. 2–4), because the God who pursues is the Creator who touches the earth and it melts (vv. 5–6). The exodus does not set Israel apart from nations whose movements God also directed (v. 7). Then the turning point: the sinful kingdom will be destroyed, but not utterly the house of Jacob (v. 8). God will shake his people in a sieve; the sinners who said disaster would never come will die, and nothing will fall through by chance (vv. 9–10).
verseByVerse.theology: No one can hide from God's judgment, yet in judgment he preserves a remnant for himself.

verseByVerse.quote: I saw the Lord standing beside the altar, and he said: "Strike the capitals until the thresholds shake, and shatter them on the heads of all the people; and those who are left of them I will kill with the sword; not one of them shall flee away; not one of them shall escape.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the last vision the Lord stands at Israel’s altar to bring the shrine down on its worshippers, and no one will escape.

I saw the Lord standing beside the altar. This time there is no “This is what the Lord GOD showed me” (7:1; 8:1): Amos simply sees the Lord at the altar (the ESV notes it may be “on” the altar), probably the altar at Bethel, the royal shrine at the heart of Israel’s false worship (7:13). People went there to be safe with God. Now God stands there, not to accept their offerings but to judge.

Strike the capitals. The capitals were the decorated tops of the pillars that held up the roof. When they are struck, the building shudders down to its thresholds and collapses on the crowd (the ESV notes that the Hebrew reads “all of them”), and the sword hunts down any who scramble clear. The double “not one of them” closes every exit.

Religion without repentance is no refuge. The shrine Israel trusted became the place of its destruction, as Jesus later foretold of the temple in Jerusalem (Mark 13:2). But he spoke of another temple, “the temple of his body” (John 2:21), struck down at the cross and raised on the third day. In him God gives the sacrifice and the shelter that no shrine of our own making can.

Uncertain wording. The verse does not say whom the Lord commands to strike, perhaps an angel of judgment. The Hebrew of “shatter them on the heads of all the people” is compressed and translations differ, but the picture of a building falling on those inside is clear.

verseByVerse.quote: "If they dig into Sheol, from there shall my hand take them; if they climb up to heaven, from there I will bring them down. If they hide themselves on the top of Carmel, from there I will search them out and take them; and if they hide from my sight at the bottom of the sea, there I will command the serpent, and it shall bite them. And if they go into captivity before their enemies, there I will command the sword, and it shall kill them; and I will fix my eyes upon them for evil and not for good."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nowhere in all creation, from the grave to the sky and the sea floor to a foreign land, can the rebel hide from God.

If they dig into Sheol. Amos imagines every hiding place: Sheol, the realm of the dead; heaven; the top of Carmel, the wooded headland with its caves (compare 1:2); the bottom of the sea, where “the serpent” will find them at God’s command; even exile, where his sword will follow. Jonah tried the sea and learned the same lesson (Jonah 1:3).

Psalm 139 turned around. These verses echo Psalm 139: “If I ascend to heaven, you are there! If I make my bed in Sheol, you are there!” (Psalm 139:8). But the tone is reversed. For the psalmist God’s presence everywhere is comfort: “even there your hand shall lead me” (Psalm 139:10). For those running from God in rebellion the same truth is terror. The difference is not in God but in us, for “no creature is hidden from his sight” (Hebrews 4:13).

For evil and not for good. Normally “the eye of the LORD is on those who fear him” (Psalm 33:18), to protect them; here his eyes are fixed on Israel to harm them. There is only one place to hide from the judgment of God, and that is in God himself, through Christ, who bore it for us: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1).

Uncertain wording. “The serpent” at the bottom of the sea may be a sea snake, but more likely the great sea monster of Hebrew poetry (compare Isaiah 27:1). Either way it is God’s creature, obeying his command.

verseByVerse.quote: The Lord GOD of hosts, he who touches the earth and it melts, and all who dwell in it mourn, and all of it rises like the Nile, and sinks again, like the Nile of Egypt; who builds his upper chambers in the heavens and founds his vault upon the earth; who calls for the waters of the sea and pours them out upon the surface of the earth— the LORD is his name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God who pursues the guilty is the Creator, who melts the earth with a touch and rules sky and sea.

He who touches the earth and it melts. For the third time Amos breaks into a hymn (compare 4:13; 5:8–9). The God who searches out every hiding place has only to touch the earth and it melts; the land heaves like the Nile in flood (as in 8:8), and the fortresses Israel trusted are wax before him.

Who builds his upper chambers in the heavens. God’s dwelling is not a shrine at Bethel but the heavens, and he commands the sea (as in 5:8). He is no local god to be kept in a box, managed or bribed. Yet this God, too great for any shrine, has made himself known in Jesus Christ, in whom “the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily” (Colossians 2:9).

Uncertain wording. The word translated “vault” is rare and elsewhere means a bundle or band; here it seems to picture the sky arched over the earth. Some translate “foundation”. Either way God has built his house above the world.

verseByVerse.quote: "Are you not like the Cushites to me, O people of Israel?" declares the LORD. "Did I not bring up Israel from the land of Egypt, and the Philistines from Caphtor and the Syrians from Kir? Behold, the eyes of the Lord GOD are upon the sinful kingdom, and I will destroy it from the surface of the ground, except that I will not utterly destroy the house of Jacob," declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The exodus did not make Israel untouchable, for God directs every nation’s history; he will destroy the sinful kingdom, but not utterly the house of Jacob.

Are you not like the Cushites to me? The question would have shocked Israel. The Cushites lived far to the south, along the upper Nile beyond Egypt. Israel thought the exodus made them untouchable. Yes, God brought Israel out of Egypt, but he also directed the movements of other nations: he brought the Philistines from Caphtor (probably Crete; compare Deuteronomy 2:23) and the Syrians from Kir (compare 1:5).

The limits of privilege. A people who forget God’s grace and live like the nations will be treated like the nations. God rules all history: “he made from one man every nation of mankind” and determined “the boundaries of their dwelling place” (Acts 17:26). There is also a hidden hope here. The God who directed Cushites and Philistines will one day gather people from every nation (v. 12).

What it does not mean. Not that Israel’s election was unreal. “You only have I known of all the families of the earth”, Amos said, but the conclusion was “therefore I will punish you” (3:2). Privilege, like church membership or a Christian home today, is a real gift but no shelter for those who despise the Giver.

I will not utterly destroy the house of Jacob. God would wipe out the sinful kingdom, Israel as a political power, and he did; the northern kingdom never returned. Then comes the word that changes everything: “except that I will not utterly destroy the house of Jacob”. God’s promise to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob will not fail. The kingdom will fall, but the people of God will not come to an end. This is the turning point of the book, and Paul saw the same in his day: “at the present time there is a remnant, chosen by grace” (Romans 11:5).
verseByVerse.note: Caphtor is probably Crete; Kir was probably in Mesopotamia; its exact site is unknown.

verseByVerse.quote: "For behold, I will command, and shake the house of Israel among all the nations as one shakes with a sieve, but no pebble shall fall to the earth. All the sinners of my people shall die by the sword, who say, 'Disaster shall not overtake or meet us.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will shake his people among the nations like grain in a sieve: the complacent sinners will die, and nothing will fall through by chance.

As one shakes with a sieve. How can God both destroy and preserve? With a sieve. After grain was threshed and winnowed, it was shaken in a sieve to separate it from stones and rubbish. God will shake Israel “among all the nations” in exile, and his sifting will be exact: “no pebble shall fall to the earth.” No sinner will escape, and not one of God’s own will be lost.

All the sinners of my people. Who is caught in the sieve? “All the sinners of my people”, those who say, “Disaster shall not overtake or meet us.” Their sin was not only what they did but their confidence that God’s warnings would never come true. Belonging outwardly to God’s people saves no one who persists in unbelief.

Comfort for the shaken. The same picture comforts Christians in hard times. Jesus told Peter, “Satan demanded to have you, that he might sift you like wheat, but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22:31–32). Trials shake us, but they cannot shake a true believer out of Christ’s hand: “no one will snatch them out of my hand” (John 10:28).

Uncertain wording. The word translated “pebble” can mean a small stone (2 Samuel 17:13) or perhaps a kernel, and the kind of sieve is uncertain. A coarse sieve that holds back stones would mean no sinner slips through; a fine one that holds the grain would mean no true grain is lost. Both fit the chapter (vv. 8, 10).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–15 — I Will Raise Up the Booth of David
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After judgment, grace has the last word: God will restore David’s kingdom, gather the nations into it and give his people a home and a harvest that never end. The booth of David, the royal house reduced to a collapsing shelter, will be raised and rebuilt as in the days of old (v. 11), and it will take in the remnant of Edom and all the nations called by God’s name (v. 12). The land will be so fruitful that ploughing catches up with reaping and the mountains drip with wine (v. 13). The curses of exile are reversed, with ruined cities rebuilt and vineyards enjoyed (v. 14), and God plants his people where they will never again be uprooted, for he is still “the LORD your God” (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: God's last word is grace: through the Son of David he gathers a people from all nations into a kingdom that will never end.

verseByVerse.quote: "In that day I will raise up the booth of David that is fallen and repair its breaches, and raise up its ruins and rebuild it as in the days of old, that they may possess the remnant of Edom and all the nations who are called by my name," declares the LORD who does this.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will raise up David’s fallen royal house and through it bring the nations, even Israel’s enemies, under his name: a promise kept in Jesus Christ.

In that day. After chapters of judgment, the sun breaks through. The day of the LORD that was “darkness, and not light” for the rebellious (5:18) becomes a day of restoration.

The booth of David that is fallen. A booth was a simple shelter of branches, the kind of hut used at harvest time and at the Feast of Booths. The picture is humbling: David’s royal house, his dynasty, so broken that it looks like a flimsy hut collapsing in a field. It had already lost ten tribes, and worse was coming: Judah’s kings went into exile, and no son of David sat on a throne again. But God will rebuild it “as in the days of old”.

The remnant of Edom. The restored kingdom will take in “the remnant of Edom”, Israel’s old enemy, descended from Esau (1:11), “and all the nations who are called by my name”. To be called by God’s name means to belong to him (Deuteronomy 28:10), much as a conqueror gave a captured city his own name (2 Samuel 12:28). David had once ruled Edom by force (2 Samuel 8:14). The greater Son of David would gather the nations to belong to God.

Fulfilled in Christ. This promise was kept in Jesus. The angel told Mary, “the Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever” (Luke 1:32–33). Peter preached that David foresaw “the resurrection of the Christ” (Acts 2:30–31). When God raised Jesus from the dead and seated him at his right hand, he raised up the fallen house of David. Jesus calls himself “the root and the descendant of David” (Revelation 22:16).

The Jerusalem council. When the early church had to decide whether Gentiles must become Jews to follow Christ, James quoted Amos: “I will rebuild the tent of David that has fallen … that the remnant of mankind may seek the Lord, and all the Gentiles who are called by my name” (Acts 15:16–17). He saw the promise coming true as Gentiles believed in Jesus, and every Gentile believer is part of its answer: “you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ” (Ephesians 2:13).

Where Christians differ. Many in the Reformed tradition believe that Acts 15 shows the promise being fulfilled now: Christ reigns as David’s Son, and the Gentiles coming into the church are the nations called by God’s name. Many dispensational Christians agree that Acts 15 is in harmony with the prophecy, but believe its complete fulfilment awaits a future earthly kingdom when Christ reigns from Jerusalem. This commentary’s view: the first reading is the more likely, because James cites the promise to settle a question about the church in his own day. All agree that Jesus is the promised Son of David, gathering people from every nation.

Textual note. James’s wording differs from the Hebrew mainly because he quotes the Greek translation of the Old Testament (as the ESV notes). The Greek reads “the remnant of mankind” where the Hebrew has “the remnant of Edom”. In Hebrew, Edom and mankind (adam) are spelled almost alike, and the verbs for “possess” and “seek” differ by one letter, which probably explains the Greek. The meaning is the same: the nations will come under the rule of David’s Son.
verseByVerse.note: The Hebrew word for booth (sukkah) is the word that gives the Feast of Booths its name (Lev 23:42).

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, the days are coming," declares the LORD, "when the plowman shall overtake the reaper and the treader of grapes him who sows the seed; the mountains shall drip sweet wine, and all the hills shall flow with it. I will restore the fortunes of my people Israel, and they shall rebuild the ruined cities and inhabit them; they shall plant vineyards and drink their wine, and they shall make gardens and eat their fruit. I will plant them on their land, and they shall never again be uprooted out of the land that I have given them," says the LORD your God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God promises his restored people a land so fruitful that the harvests overlap, every curse of exile reversed, and a home from which they will never again be uprooted.

The plowman shall overtake the reaper. The book that began with pastures withering (1:2) ends in abundance. Grain was reaped in spring, grapes trodden in late summer, and fields ploughed and sown in autumn; here the reapers are still at work when the ploughman arrives, and the treader in the winepress is still busy when sowing begins. God’s law had promised such blessing for obedience: “Your threshing shall last to the time of the grape harvest” (Leviticus 26:5). “The mountains shall drip sweet wine”, as Joel also foresaw (Joel 3:18). Locusts, drought and blight (4:6–11) give way to endless plenty.

They shall plant vineyards and drink their wine. Every curse is reversed. God had said, “you have planted pleasant vineyards, but you shall not drink their wine” (5:11). Now they will. What sin destroyed, grace restores, as in Isaiah’s picture of the new creation: “They shall build houses and inhabit them; they shall plant vineyards and eat their fruit” (Isaiah 65:21).

I will plant them on their land. God himself will plant his people like a tree, never again to be uprooted. And the final words matter: “the LORD your God”. After all the judgment, he is still their God. The covenant stands.

The shape of the book. Amos began with a lion’s roar (1:2) and ends with a harvest that never stops. Between the two stands the Son of David, who took the roar of judgment on himself at the cross and rose to reign for ever. In him God’s people will be planted in a new creation, where “the dwelling place of God is with man” (Revelation 21:3). Whatever our view of the details, God’s final word to his people is not judgment but home.

Where Christians differ. Some Christians believe this promises a future restoration of the Jewish people to the land in a coming earthly kingdom, and many godly believers see God’s hand in their modern return to it. Many in the Reformed tradition believe the land promise is fulfilled and enlarged in Christ: Abraham was promised that he would be “heir of the world” (Romans 4:13), and God’s people look for “a better country, that is, a heavenly one” (Hebrews 11:16), the new heavens and new earth. Many also expect a great turning of Jewish people to Christ before the end (Romans 11:25–26). This commentary’s view: the promise is fulfilled in Christ and completed in the new creation, because the New Testament reads the land promises this way; the modern state of Israel is not its fulfilment. With humility it holds that Romans 11 most naturally looks for a future turning of many Jewish people to Christ, within the one people of God, and that Christians should love the Jewish people and pray for their salvation. Faithful believers differ here, and this commentary honours those who read the promise otherwise.

9.title: The Booth of David
9.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 9 closes the book. It brings the last of Amos’s five visions, and then, after nine chapters in which judgment has hardly let up, the book ends in hope.

The message. God cannot be escaped, and the privileges of his people do not shelter them from his judgment; but judgment is not his last word. He will sift his people so that no sinner escapes and none of his own is lost, and out of the ruins he will raise the fallen house of David, gather the nations under it and plant his people in a home they will never lose.

Why it was said. Israel felt safe: its shrines were busy, the exodus seemed a guarantee, and people said, “Disaster shall not overtake or meet us” (v. 10; see the introduction). Amos takes away every hiding place. Yet those who lived through the fall of Samaria and the exile also needed to know that God had not finished with his people.

How the chapter makes its case. The Lord stands at the altar and orders the shrine brought down on the worshippers (v. 1). There is no hiding place anywhere, from the grave to the sea floor to exile (vv. 2–4), for the God who judges made and rules it all (vv. 5–6). The exodus gives Israel no more immunity than the Philistines’ or Syrians’ migrations (v. 7). The sinful kingdom will be destroyed, but not utterly the house of Jacob (v. 8): God will shake it in a sieve, and the confident sinners will die (vv. 9–10). Then the tone changes. “In that day” God will raise up David’s fallen booth and bring the nations under it (vv. 11–12), and the land will yield harvests so large that the seasons overlap, with his people planted there for ever (vv. 13–15).

Where it leads. Above all by promise. David’s fallen booth was raised when God raised Jesus, David’s Son, and set him on the throne; James quoted this passage as Gentiles turned to Christ (Acts 15:16–17). It also exposes a need: if no one can hide from God, we need a hiding place God himself provides, and we find it in the one who bore his judgment. And the sifting that loses none of God’s own is the work of the Shepherd who said, “no one will snatch them out of my hand” (John 10:28).

For us. No religion, church membership or godly upbringing hides anyone from God; take shelter in Christ, the Son of David, on whom his judgment has already fallen. And look ahead with hope: God’s last word to his people is not ruin but a King, a harvest and a home from which they will never be uprooted.
9.theology:
No one can escape God's judgment, and false worship becomes the place where it falls (vv. 1-4; Heb 4:13).

God's presence everywhere is terror to the rebel and comfort to the one who trusts him (vv. 2-4; Ps 139:7-10; Ps 33:18).

God rules the history of all nations, and past privilege gives no licence to sin (v. 7; Acts 17:26).

In judgment God preserves a remnant, and none of his own will be lost (vv. 8-9; Luke 22:31-32; John 10:27-29).

God keeps his promise to David by raising up Jesus Christ, David's Son, to reign forever (v. 11; Luke 1:32-33; Acts 2:30-31; Rev 22:16).

The kingdom of David's Son includes people from all nations, as the apostles recognised in the inclusion of the Gentiles (v. 12; Acts 15:13-18; Eph 2:12-13; Rev 7:9).

God's final word to his people is restoration: every curse reversed and a home from which they will never be uprooted, fulfilled in the new creation (vv. 13-15; Lev 26:5; Isa 65:21-22; Rom 4:13; Heb 11:16; Rev 21:3-4).
9.examples:
A temple collapses on the worshippers who trusted in it, and a fugitive hiding at the bottom of the sea finds God already there. Yet the sieve that shakes Israel lets not one grain be lost, and that is the comfort of every believer who is being shaken now.

A collapsed shelter in a field becomes a royal house, and a council in Jerusalem reads Amos as Gentiles come to faith. The harvest grows so large that the ploughman catches up with the reapers, and this time those who plant vineyards drink the wine.

keyVerse.quote: In that day I will raise up the booth of David that is fallen and repair its breaches, and raise up its ruins and rebuild it as in the days of old
keyVerse.note: This verse is the hinge on which the book turns from judgment to hope. David’s royal house, reduced to a collapsing hut, will be raised by God himself, and the New Testament sees the promise kept when God raised Jesus, David’s Son, and began gathering the nations under his rule (Acts 15:16–17).

9.reflection:
Israel trusted its shrine, its exodus and its place as God’s people to keep it safe (vv. 1, 7, 10). What “safe places” do people rely on today, inside the church and outside it? Why is none of them a refuge from God?

Verses 2–4 make God’s presence everywhere a terror, while Psalm 139 makes it a comfort. What makes the difference, and how does Christ change which of these is true for us?

God sifts his people so that “no pebble shall fall to the earth” (v. 9), and Jesus prayed for Peter when Satan asked to sift him (Luke 22:31–32). How does this help a believer going through a time of shaking?

James saw Amos 9:11–12 coming true as Gentiles came to Christ (Acts 15:16–17). How should it shape our view of the church, and our hope for the future, that God’s last word in Amos is a restored King, a gathered world and a home that will never be lost?
